\title{A Finite-Set Escape Program for the \(L^2\) Benjamini-Schramm Conjecture}
\author{Working draft}
\date{Started 2026-06-08}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This is a working manuscript for a long-term attempt to prove the
Benjamini-Schramm non-uniqueness conjecture for Bernoulli bond percolation on
nonamenable quasi-transitive graphs.  The stronger target is the \(L^2\)
operator inequality \(\pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G)\), where \(p_{2\to2}\) is the
boundedness threshold of the two-point function \(T_p(x,y)=\Pp(x\leftrightarrow
y)\) on \(\ell^2(V)\).  A theorem of Hutchcroft reduces this stronger target to
a mean-field susceptibility estimate and a finite-set escape condition for the
subcritical two-point kernel.  The present draft records the selected open
problem, the verified status, the operator formulation, and several elementary
reductions that isolate the remaining obstruction.  It does not yet claim a
solution of the global conjecture.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents

\section{Status of the project}

The objective of this project is to solve a major open problem in probability
theory, write the solution as a full \LaTeX{} paper, and compile a PDF.  The
target selected here is the Benjamini-Schramm non-uniqueness conjecture for
Bernoulli bond percolation on nonamenable quasi-transitive graphs
\cite{BenjaminiSchramm1996}.  The problem is both classical and active: recent
work continues to solve important subclasses and threshold phenomena rather
than the full generality \cite{HutchcroftPan2024Relativization,
HutchcroftPan2024Dimension,TerlovTimar2025Weighted,Li2026Planar}.

The present manuscript is not a final solution.  It is a structured research
draft whose purpose is to make the target precise enough that subsequent proof
attempts have a clear place to attach.  The paper deliberately separates
proved reductions from conjectural bridges.

\subsection{Open-status audit}

The current-status audit used for this draft has three layers.  First, the
local solved-problem register in the surrounding workspace records solved work
on Gaussian phase retrieval, Balan-Wang type stability, Plucker reductions, and
related random-matrix questions.  It does not record a percolation theorem of
the kind studied here.  Second, the main modern reference for the operator
route \cite{Hutchcroft2019Hyperbolic} states Conjecture~\ref{conj:bs} and then
solves it only under additional large-scale geometric assumptions, most
prominently Gromov hyperbolicity.  Third, the recent papers located during the
audit continue to prove special classes or adjacent threshold phenomena
\cite{HutchcroftPan2024Relativization,HutchcroftPan2024Dimension,Li2026Planar}.
No source found in the 2026-06-08 search announced a general proof of
\(\pc<\pu\), or of the stronger \(\pc<p_{2\to2}\), for every nonamenable
quasi-transitive graph.

This matters methodologically.  The project should not spend effort proving a
statement already known under a different name, and it should not confuse a
planar-site conjecture with the bond-percolation quasi-transitive conjecture.
The target here is deliberately the general bond-percolation statement, with
the \(L^2\) threshold as the preferred route.

\subsection{Success standard}

A final solution would need at least the following components.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{S\arabic*.},leftmargin=2.5em]
  \item A precise theorem statement covering all connected, locally finite,
  quasi-transitive, nonamenable graphs, or a clearly stronger theorem that
  implies that statement.
  \item A proof that does not assume hidden extra hypotheses such as
  hyperbolicity, planarity, nonunimodularity, product structure, property
  \(T\), or existence of harmonic Dirichlet functions.
  \item A check against amenable quasi-transitive graphs, where
  \(\pc=\pu\), to confirm that the argument uses nonamenability at the right
  point.
  \item A literature comparison explaining why the theorem is not subsumed by
  existing special-case results.
  \item A complete \LaTeX{} manuscript and a compiled PDF.
\end{enumerate}

The current draft satisfies only the setup and reduction parts of this list.
The main proof is still missing.

\section{Percolation background}

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected, locally finite, infinite graph.  Bernoulli bond
percolation at parameter \(p\in[0,1]\) keeps each edge independently with
probability \(p\) and deletes it otherwise.  We write \(G[p]\) for the resulting
random subgraph and write \(x\leftrightarrow y\) for the event that \(x\) and
\(y\) lie in the same open cluster.

The critical probability and uniqueness threshold are
\[
  \pc(G)=\inf\{p:\Pp(G[p]\text{ has an infinite cluster})=1\}
\]
and
\[
  \pu(G)=\inf\{p:\Pp(G[p]\text{ has a unique infinite cluster})=1\}.
\]
For quasi-transitive graphs, the number of infinite clusters is almost surely
\(0\), \(1\), or \(\infty\), and the interval \((\pc,\pu)\), when non-empty, is
the non-uniqueness phase.

A graph is quasi-transitive if its automorphism group has finitely many orbits
on \(V\).  It is nonamenable if its Cheeger constant is positive:
\[
  h(G)=\inf_{K\subset V\text{ finite}}
  \frac{|\partial_E K|}{\sum_{x\in K}\deg(x)}>0.
\]
Here \(\partial_EK\) denotes the set of edges with one endpoint in \(K\) and one
endpoint outside \(K\).

\begin{conjecture}[Benjamini-Schramm]
\label{conj:bs}
Let \(G\) be a connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive graph.  Then
\[
  \pc(G)<\pu(G)
\]
if and only if \(G\) is nonamenable.
\end{conjecture}

The amenable direction is known: amenable quasi-transitive graphs satisfy
\(\pc=\pu\).  The hard direction is to prove \(\pc<\pu\) for every
nonamenable quasi-transitive graph.  Major positive cases include nonamenable
planar quasi-transitive graphs, nonunimodular transitive graphs, hyperbolic
quasi-transitive graphs, and several group-theoretic and product classes
\cite{Hutchcroft2019Hyperbolic,HermonHutchcroft2021,
HutchcroftPan2024Relativization,HutchcroftPan2024Dimension}.

\section{\texorpdfstring{The \(L^2\) strengthening}{The L2 strengthening}}

For \(p<\pc\), define the two-point function
\[
  T_p(x,y)=\tau_p(x,y)=\Pp(x\leftrightarrow y).
\]
We view \(T_p\) as a positive symmetric kernel on \(V\).  Its susceptibility
row sum is
\[
  \chi_p(x)=\sum_{y\in V}\tau_p(x,y),
  \qquad
  \chiBar_p=\sup_{x\in V}\chi_p(x).
\]
For quasi-transitive graphs, \(\chiBar_p<\infty\) for \(p<\pc\) and diverges as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).

Following Hutchcroft \cite{Hutchcroft2019Hyperbolic}, define
\[
  p_{2\to2}(G)=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:T_p\text{ is bounded on }\ell^2(V)\}.
\]
For quasi-transitive graphs,
\[
  \pc(G)\le p_{2\to2}(G)\le \pu(G).
\]
Thus the following conjecture strengthens Conjecture~\ref{conj:bs}.

\begin{conjecture}[\texorpdfstring{\(L^2\)}{L2} Benjamini-Schramm]
\label{conj:l2bs}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive, and nonamenable.
Then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{conjecture}

This formulation is attractive because \(p_{2\to2}\) can be attacked by
functional analysis of the two-point operator.  It also has a useful finite-set
criterion, recalled next.

\section{Hutchcroft's finite-set criterion}

The next theorem is a restatement of the criterion developed in
\cite{Hutchcroft2019Hyperbolic}.  It is included here to fix notation and to
identify the precise obstruction that this project attempts to remove.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-set criterion]
\label{thm:hutchcroft-criterion}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and quasi-transitive.  Suppose that
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}(\pc-p)\chiBar_p<\infty
  \tag{MF}
  \label{eq:mf}
\]
and
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite}}
  \frac{\sum_{x,y\in K}\tau_p(x,y)}{\chiBar_p |K|}=0.
  \tag{FE}
  \label{eq:fe}
\]
Then \(\pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G)\).  In particular \(\pc(G)<\pu(G)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
Condition \eqref{eq:mf} is a mean-field susceptibility upper bound.  Condition
\eqref{eq:fe} is the finite-set escape condition: after normalizing by the
maximal row sum, no finite set can retain a positive fraction of the
two-point mass as \(p\uparrow\pc\).
\end{remark}

The known hyperbolic proof verifies these two conditions using large-scale
geometry.  The open problem is whether nonamenability alone is enough.

\section{Normalized kernels}

Define the normalized two-point kernel
\[
  Q_p(x,y)=\frac{\tau_p(x,y)}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
Then \(Q_p\) is a positive symmetric kernel satisfying
\[
  \sup_x\sum_y Q_p(x,y)\le1.
\]
The finite-set escape condition becomes
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\eta_p=0,
  \qquad
  \eta_p=
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite}}
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Elementary bounds for \(Q_p\)]
\label{lem:q-basic}
For every \(p<\pc\), the kernel \(Q_p\) is positive, symmetric, and satisfies
\[
  \norm{Q_p}_{1\to1}\le1,\qquad
  \norm{Q_p}_{\infty\to\infty}\le1,\qquad
  \norm{Q_p}_{2\to2}\le1.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first two bounds follow from symmetry and from the definition of
\(\chiBar_p\):
\[
  \sup_x\sum_y Q_p(x,y)
  =
  \chiBar_p^{-1}\sup_x\sum_y\tau_p(x,y)
  \le1.
\]
Since \(Q_p\) is symmetric, the same bound holds for column sums.  The
\(\ell^2\) bound follows by interpolation, or by the Schur test.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Failure extraction]
\label{lem:failure-extraction}
If finite-set escape fails, then there exist \(\epsilon>0\), parameters
\(p_n\uparrow\pc\), finite non-empty sets \(K_n\subset V\), and functions
\[
  f_n=|K_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_{K_n}
\]
such that \(\norm{f_n}_2=1\) and
\[
  \ip{f_n}{Q_{p_n}f_n}\ge\epsilon
\]
for every \(n\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If finite-set escape fails, then for some \(\epsilon>0\) there are
\(p_n\uparrow\pc\) and finite non-empty \(K_n\) with
\[
  |K_n|^{-1}\sum_{x,y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}(x,y)\ge\epsilon.
\]
For \(f_n=|K_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_{K_n}\), symmetry and positivity give
\[
  \ip{f_n}{Q_{p_n}f_n}
  =
  |K_n|^{-1}\sum_{x,y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}(x,y),
\]
which is at least \(\epsilon\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Lemma~\ref{lem:failure-extraction} is elementary, but it is the correct
starting point for a contradiction proof.  The hard task is to convert large
\(\ip{f_n}{Q_{p_n}f_n}\) into almost-invariance for the graph random walk, or
into another object forbidden by nonamenability.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Failure has spectral content]
\label{lem:spectral-content}
If finite-set escape fails, then there are \(p_n\uparrow\pc\) such that
\[
   \liminf_{n\to\infty}\norm{Q_{p_n}}_{2\to2}>0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
   \liminf_{n\to\infty}
   \frac{\norm{T_{p_n}}_{2\to2}}{\chiBar_{p_n}}>0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:failure-extraction}, failure of escape gives unit vectors
\(f_n\) with \(\ip{f_n}{Q_{p_n}f_n}\ge\epsilon\).  Hence
\[
   \norm{Q_{p_n}}_{2\to2}\ge \ip{f_n}{Q_{p_n}f_n}\ge\epsilon.
\]
The second display is just \(Q_p=T_p/\chiBar_p\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The converse is false in general: a positive lower bound on
\(\norm{Q_p}_{2\to2}\) need not be witnessed by normalized indicators of finite
sets.  The finite-set formulation is stronger and is tuned to the
isoperimetric contradiction one wants from nonamenability.
\end{remark}

\section{A finite-volume boundary decomposition}

The previous lemmas say what failure of finite-set escape gives at the level
of the normalized kernel.  The next proposition opens that event up using the
geometry of a finite set.  It is the first non-tautological reduction in this
draft.

For a finite set \(K\subset V\), let \(\tau_p^K(x,y)\) be the probability that
\(x\) and \(y\) are connected by an open path using only edges of the induced
subgraph on \(K\).  Define
\[
  \chi_p^K(x)=\sum_{y\in K}\tau_p^K(x,y),
  \qquad
  S_p(K)=\sum_{x,y\in K}\tau_p^K(x,y).
\]
Let
\[
  \partial^+K=\{(a,b): a\in K,\ b\notin K,\ a\sim b\}
\]
be the oriented edge boundary, always oriented from inside \(K\) to outside
\(K\).

\begin{proposition}[Last-exit boundary decomposition]
\label{prop:last-exit}
For every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) and every \(p\in[0,1]\),
\[
  \sum_{x,y\in K}\tau_p(x,y)
  \le
  S_p(K)
  +
  p^2
  \sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\partial^+K\\(d,c)\in\partial^+K}}
  \chi_p^K(a)\,\tau_p(b,c)\,\chi_p^K(d).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(x,y\in K\).  If \(x\) is connected to \(y\) by a path contained in \(K\),
the event contributes to \(\tau_p^K(x,y)\).  Otherwise choose a self-avoiding
open path \(\gamma\) from \(x\) to \(y\) that is not contained in \(K\).  Let
\((a,b)\in\partial^+K\) be the first oriented boundary edge crossed by
\(\gamma\), and let \((d,c)\in\partial^+K\) be the last oriented boundary edge
crossed by \(\gamma\), where the actual last crossing is from \(c\notin K\) to
\(d\in K\).

The path \(\gamma\) decomposes into five edge-disjoint pieces: an internal
path in \(K\) from \(x\) to \(a\), the boundary edge \(ab\), the middle segment
from \(b\) to \(c\), the boundary edge \(cd\), and an internal path in \(K\)
from \(d\) to \(y\).  The middle segment need not stay outside \(K\); it may
make further excursions through \(K\).  This is why the middle two-point
function below is the ambient \(\tau_p(b,c)\), not a complement-restricted
two-point function.

Thus \(\gamma\) witnesses the disjoint occurrence of the following five
increasing events: \(x\) is connected to \(a\) inside \(K\), the edge \(ab\) is
open, \(b\) is connected to \(c\) in \(G\), the edge \(cd\) is open, and \(d\)
is connected to \(y\) inside \(K\).  By the BK inequality, or equivalently the
standard disjoint-occurrence bound for increasing connection events
\cite{Grimmett1999}, the probability of this contribution is at most
\[
  \tau_p^K(x,a)\,p\,\tau_p(b,c)\,p\,\tau_p^K(d,y).
\]
Taking the union bound over the possible first and last boundary crossings
gives
\[
  \tau_p(x,y)
  \le
  \tau_p^K(x,y)
  +
  p^2
  \sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\partial^+K\\(d,c)\in\partial^+K}}
  \tau_p^K(x,a)\tau_p(b,c)\tau_p^K(d,y).
\]
Summing over \(x,y\in K\) and using symmetry of \(\tau_p^K\) gives the stated
inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Interior-boundary dichotomy]
\label{cor:interior-boundary}
Let \(Q_p=\tau_p/\chiBar_p\).  If, for some finite non-empty \(K\subset V\),
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)\ge\epsilon,
\]
then at least one of the following two alternatives holds:
\[
  S_p(K)\ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}\chiBar_p |K|
  \tag{I}
  \label{eq:interior-alt}
\]
or
\[
  p^2
  \sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\partial^+K\\(d,c)\in\partial^+K}}
  \chi_p^K(a)\,Q_p(b,c)\,\chi_p^K(d)
  \ge
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}|K|.
  \tag{B}
  \label{eq:boundary-alt}
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Divide the inequality of Proposition~\ref{prop:last-exit} by
\(\chiBar_p|K|\).  If the normalized left-hand side is at least \(\epsilon\),
then the normalized interior term or the normalized boundary-transfer term is
at least \(\epsilon/2\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Boundary \(L^2\)-mass obstruction]
\label{cor:boundary-l2}
For \(z\in V\setminus K\), define the boundary susceptibility weight
\[
  \mu_{p,K}(z)=\sum_{\substack{a\in K\\ a\sim z}}\chi_p^K(a),
\]
and set \(\mu_{p,K}(z)=0\) for \(z\in K\).  If the boundary alternative
\eqref{eq:boundary-alt} holds and \(p>0\), then
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_2^2
  \ge
  \frac{\epsilon}{2p^2}|K|
  \ge
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}|K|.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The boundary term in \eqref{eq:boundary-alt} can be written as
\[
  p^2\sum_{b,c\in V}\mu_{p,K}(b)Q_p(b,c)\mu_{p,K}(c)
  =
  p^2\ip{\mu_{p,K}}{Q_p\mu_{p,K}}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:q-basic}, \(Q_p\) is a contraction on \(\ell^2(V)\).  Hence
\[
  \ip{\mu_{p,K}}{Q_p\mu_{p,K}}\le \|\mu_{p,K}\|_2^2.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:boundary-alt} gives the first inequality.  The
second follows from \(p\le1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Corollary~\ref{cor:interior-boundary} is useful because it splits the hard
finite-set escape problem into two more concrete obstructions.  The interior
alternative says that the finite induced subgraph on \(K\) already has
susceptibility comparable to the ambient near-critical susceptibility.  The
boundary alternative says that the finite-volume susceptibility weights on the
edge boundary have large mutual interaction through the ambient graph.
Corollary~\ref{cor:boundary-l2} shows that this can happen only if those
boundary susceptibility weights have large \(\ell^2\)-mass.  A complete proof
of finite-set escape must rule out the interior alternative and this boundary
\(\ell^2\)-mass obstruction uniformly near criticality on nonamenable
quasi-transitive graphs.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Interior term via killed self-avoiding paths}

For a finite \(K\subset V\), let \(c_n^K(x)\) be the number of self-avoiding
paths of length \(n\) starting at \(x\) and using only vertices of \(K\), and
let
\[
  A_n(K)=\frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x\in K}c_n^K(x).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Killed path-count bound]
\label{lem:killed-saw}
For every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) and every \(p\in[0,1]\),
\[
  \frac{S_p(K)}{|K|}
  \le
  \sum_{n\ge0}p^n A_n(K).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(x\) is connected to \(y\) inside \(K\), then there is an open
self-avoiding path inside \(K\) from \(x\) to \(y\).  Taking the union bound
over all such paths gives
\[
  \tau_p^K(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{\gamma:x\to y\text{ s.a.w. in }K} p^{|\gamma|}.
\]
Summing over \(y\in K\) and then over \(x\in K\) gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Interior escape from killed-growth control]
\label{prop:interior-killed-growth}
Assume that there are constants \(C<\infty\) and \(\theta<1/\pc(G)\) such
that
\[
  A_n(K)\le C\theta^n
\]
for every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) and every \(n\ge0\).  If
\(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\), then
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\sup_K
  \frac{S_p(K)}{\chiBar_p|K|}=0.
\]
In particular, the interior alternative \eqref{eq:interior-alt} is ruled out
uniformly near criticality.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(p_0<\pc\) so close to \(\pc\) that \(p_0\theta<1\).  For
\(p\in[p_0,\pc)\), Lemma~\ref{lem:killed-saw} gives
\[
  \frac{S_p(K)}{|K|}
  \le
  \sum_{n\ge0}p^n A_n(K)
  \le
  C\sum_{n\ge0}(p\theta)^n
  \le
  \frac{C}{1-\pc\theta}.
\]
The right-hand side is independent of \(K\) and \(p\).  Dividing by
\(\chiBar_p\) and using \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Proposition~\ref{prop:interior-killed-growth} gives a concrete intermediate
target: prove a uniform killed-self-avoiding-walk growth rate strictly below
\(1/\pc\).  This is much stronger than nonamenability as stated, but it is a
clear route to a publishable special-case theorem if it can be verified in a
new class of nonamenable quasi-transitive graphs.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Deterministic boundary-weight bounds}

Let
\[
  \partial_{\mathrm{in}}K=\{a\in K:\exists z\notin K,\ a\sim z\},
  \qquad
  B_p(K)=\sum_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}\chi_p^K(a),
\]
and
\[
  M_p(K)=\max_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}\chi_p^K(a),
\]
with \(M_p(K)=0\) if \(\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K=\varnothing\).

\begin{lemma}[Boundary-weight norm bounds]
\label{lem:boundary-norms}
If \(G\) has maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), then for every finite
non-empty \(K\subset V\),
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_1\le \Delta B_p(K)\le \Delta S_p(K),
\]
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_\infty\le \Delta M_p(K),
\]
and
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_2^2
  \le
  \Delta^2\sum_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}\chi_p^K(a)^2
  \le
  \Delta^2 M_p(K)B_p(K)
  \le
  \Delta^2 M_p(K)S_p(K).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the \(L^1\) bound,
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_1
  =
  \sum_{z\notin K}\sum_{\substack{a\in K\\a\sim z}}\chi_p^K(a)
  =
  \sum_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}
  \deg_{V\setminus K}(a)\chi_p^K(a)
  \le \Delta B_p(K).
\]
The \(L^\infty\) bound follows from
\[
  \mu_{p,K}(z)
  =
  \sum_{\substack{a\in K\\a\sim z}}\chi_p^K(a)
  \le \Delta M_p(K).
\]
Finally, by Cauchy's inequality at each exterior vertex \(z\),
\[
  \mu_{p,K}(z)^2
  \le
  \deg_K(z)\sum_{\substack{a\in K\\a\sim z}}\chi_p^K(a)^2
  \le
  \Delta\sum_{\substack{a\in K\\a\sim z}}\chi_p^K(a)^2.
\]
Summing over \(z\notin K\) gives
\[
  \|\mu_{p,K}\|_2^2
  \le
  \Delta\sum_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}
  \deg_{V\setminus K}(a)\chi_p^K(a)^2
  \le
  \Delta^2\sum_{a\in\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K}\chi_p^K(a)^2.
\]
The remaining inequalities use
\(\chi_p^K(a)\le M_p(K)\) on \(\partial_{\mathrm{in}}K\) and
\(B_p(K)\le S_p(K)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[What the boundary alternative forces]
\label{cor:boundary-forces}
Assume \(G\) has maximum degree at most \(\Delta\).  If the boundary
alternative \eqref{eq:boundary-alt} holds, then
\[
  M_p(K)B_p(K)\ge \frac{\epsilon}{2p^2\Delta^2}|K|.
\]
In particular,
\[
  M_p(K)S_p(K)\ge \frac{\epsilon}{2p^2\Delta^2}|K|.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Combine Corollary~\ref{cor:boundary-l2} with
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-norms}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Corollary~\ref{cor:boundary-forces} also explains a limitation of this route.
Plain nonamenability gives a lower bound on the number of boundary edges, not
an upper bound on the susceptibility-weighted boundary quantities \(B_p(K)\)
or \(M_p(K)B_p(K)\).  Thus a proof cannot close the boundary alternative by
quoting the Cheeger inequality alone.  It must use how \(Q_p\) distributes
mass across the boundary, or it must prove a new estimate controlling the
finite-volume susceptibility profile near the boundary.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A combined finite-set escape criterion}

The preceding estimates can be summarized as a criterion that is weaker than
the full Benjamini-Schramm conjecture but strong enough to define a concrete
intermediate theorem.

Define the killed connective constant
\[
  \kappa_{\mathrm{kill}}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
  \left(\sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite}} A_n(K)\right)^{1/n}.
\]
For a finite \(K\), define the normalized boundary energy
\[
  \mathcal E_p(K)
  =
  \frac{p^2}{|K|}\ip{\mu_{p,K}}{Q_p\mu_{p,K}}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Finite-set escape criterion]
\label{thm:finite-escape-criterion}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive, and of bounded
degree.  Suppose that
\[
  \kappa_{\mathrm{kill}}(G)<1/\pc(G),
  \tag{KCG}
  \label{eq:kcg}
\]
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite}}\mathcal E_p(K)=0,
  \tag{BE}
  \label{eq:be}
\]
and \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\).  Then finite-set escape holds:
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite}}
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)=0.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  By \eqref{eq:kcg}, choose
\(\theta<1/\pc\) and \(C<\infty\) such that \(A_n(K)\le C\theta^n\) for all
finite \(K\) and all \(n\ge0\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:interior-killed-growth}
then gives a \(p_1<\pc\) such that, for \(p\in[p_1,\pc)\) and every finite
non-empty \(K\),
\[
  \frac{S_p(K)}{\chiBar_p|K|}<\epsilon/2.
\]
By \eqref{eq:be}, increasing \(p_1\) if necessary, we also have
\[
  \sup_K\mathcal E_p(K)<\epsilon/2
  \qquad p\in[p_1,\pc).
\]
For such \(p\) and \(K\), Proposition~\ref{prop:last-exit}, divided by
\(\chiBar_p|K|\), gives
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)
  \le
  \frac{S_p(K)}{\chiBar_p|K|}
  +
  \mathcal E_p(K)
  <\epsilon.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(K\) proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Conditional \(L^2\) non-uniqueness theorem]
\label{cor:conditional-l2}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive, nonamenable, and of
bounded degree.  If \eqref{eq:kcg}, \eqref{eq:be}, and the mean-field
susceptibility bound \eqref{eq:mf} hold, then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G)\le \pu(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-escape-criterion} gives finite-set escape.  Combining
finite-set escape with \eqref{eq:mf}, Theorem~\ref{thm:hutchcroft-criterion}
gives \(\pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G)\).  The inequality \(p_{2\to2}\le\pu\) was recalled
above in the \(L^2\) formulation.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The content of Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-escape-criterion} is not that
\eqref{eq:kcg} and \eqref{eq:be} are easy.  Rather, it separates the desired
finite-set escape statement into a killed path-growth problem and a
boundary-energy problem.  This is a usable framework for searching for a
publishable special case beyond the currently known hyperbolic,
nonunimodular, planar, and product settings.
\end{remark}

\section{A self-avoiding operator criterion}

The killed-growth condition controls averages over finite sets.  A stronger
but cleaner condition controls the full \(\ell^2\) operator norm of
self-avoiding-path spheres.

For \(n\ge0\), let \(C_n\) be the kernel
\[
  C_n(x,y)=
  \#\{\text{length-}n\text{ self-avoiding paths from }x\text{ to }y\}.
\]
Thus \(C_0\) is the identity kernel.  Define
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{C_n}_{2\to2}^{1/n}.
\]

\begin{proposition}[SAW operator gap criterion]
\label{prop:saw-operator-gap}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree.  If
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)<1/\pc(G),
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
If, in addition, \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\), then finite-set
escape holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\theta\) with
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}<\theta<1/\pc\).  By the definition of the limsup,
there is \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
  \norm{C_n}_{2\to2}\le C\theta^n
  \qquad n\ge0.
\]
If \(x\) is connected to \(y\), then there is an open self-avoiding path from
\(x\) to \(y\).  Hence the union bound gives the entrywise estimate
\[
  T_p(x,y)=\tau_p(x,y)\le \sum_{n\ge0}p^nC_n(x,y).
\]
The kernels involved are nonnegative and symmetric, so this entrywise
domination implies domination of \(\ell^2\) operator norms.  Indeed, for every
finitely supported \(f\),
\[
  |T_pf|\le \left(\sum_{n\ge0}p^nC_n\right)|f|
\]
pointwise.
Consequently, for every \(p<1/\theta\),
\[
  \norm{T_p}_{2\to2}
  \le
  \sum_{n\ge0}p^n\norm{C_n}_{2\to2}
  \le
  \frac{C}{1-p\theta}.
\]
Since \(1/\theta>\pc\), this proves \(p_{2\to2}>\pc\).

For the finite-set escape conclusion, fix \(p_* \in(\pc,1/\theta)\).  The
preceding bound is uniform for \(p\le\pc<p_*\).  Therefore, for every finite
non-empty \(K\),
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)
  =
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_K}{T_p\mathbf 1_K}}{\chiBar_p|K|}
  \le
  \frac{\norm{T_p}_{2\to2}}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \frac{C}{(1-p_*\theta)\chiBar_p}.
\]
Letting \(p\uparrow\pc\) proves finite-set escape.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This criterion is deliberately strong.  It replaces the finite-set problem by
a global self-avoiding-walk operator norm gap.  Its value is that it identifies
one clean mechanism that is sufficient for the \(L^2\) conjecture: an
\(\ell^2\) self-avoiding growth exponent below \(1/\pc\).  The regular-tree
calculation in Proposition~\ref{prop:killed-tree} is the model example.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Amenable stress test for the SAW criterion]
\label{prop:amenable-saw-gap-fails}
Let \(G\) be a connected transitive amenable graph of bounded degree.  Let
\(c_n\) be the number of length-\(n\) self-avoiding paths starting from a fixed
vertex, and let
\[
  \mu(G)=\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n^{1/n}
\]
be the connective constant.  Then
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)=\mu(G).
\]
Consequently the strict gap
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)<1/\pc(G)
\]
cannot hold on such a graph.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For each \(n\), the kernel \(C_n\) is nonnegative, symmetric, invariant under
the transitive automorphism group, and has row and column sums equal to
\(c_n\).  Schur's test gives
\[
  \norm{C_n}_{2\to2}\le c_n.
\]
For the reverse inequality, fix \(n\).  Amenability gives finite sets \(F_k\)
with \(|\partial F_k|/|F_k|\to0\).  Since the graph has bounded degree, the
union of all vertices within distance \(n\) of \(\partial F_k\) has size
\(o(|F_k|)\).  Thus the \(n\)-interiors
\[
  F_k^{(-n)}=\{x\in F_k:B(x,n)\subseteq F_k\}
\]
satisfy \(|F_k^{(-n)}|/|F_k|\to1\).  If \(x\in F_k^{(-n)}\), then every
length-\(n\) self-avoiding path starting from \(x\) ends in \(F_k\).  Hence
\[
  \ip{\mathbf 1_{F_k}}{C_n\mathbf 1_{F_k}}
  \ge c_n|F_k^{(-n)}|.
\]
Dividing by \(\norm{\mathbf 1_{F_k}}_2^2=|F_k|\) and letting \(k\to\infty\)
gives \(\norm{C_n}_{2\to2}\ge c_n\).  Thus
\(\norm{C_n}_{2\to2}=c_n\) for every \(n\), and taking \(n\)th roots gives
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}=\mu\).

Finally, the usual self-avoiding-path union bound implies
\[
  \pc(G)\ge1/\mu(G).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  1/\pc(G)\le\mu(G),
\]
so the strict operator gap cannot hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This proposition is a useful guardrail.  The SAW operator criterion uses
nonamenability in exactly the place where amenable Folner sets would otherwise
turn operator norm into row-sum growth.  Thus the criterion does not risk
proving \(p_c<p_{2\to2}\) on amenable transitive graphs, where
\(\pc=\pu\) and the desired non-uniqueness conclusion is false.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Cartesian product lower bound]
\label{prop:product-saw-lower}
Let \(G\) and \(H\) be connected infinite bounded-degree graphs.  Then
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G\square H)
  \ge
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)+\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(H),
\]
where \(G\square H\) denotes the Cartesian product graph.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Write \(C_n^X\) for the length-\(n\) SAW kernel on a graph \(X\).  First note
that the sequence \(\norm{C_n^X}_{2\to2}\) is submultiplicative up to the
obvious inequality
\[
  C_{m+n}^X\le C_m^XC_n^X
\]
entrywise: every length-\(m+n\) self-avoiding path splits into a length-\(m\)
self-avoiding path followed by a length-\(n\) self-avoiding path.  Positivity
then gives
\[
  \norm{C_{m+n}^X}_{2\to2}
  \le
  \norm{C_m^X}_{2\to2}\norm{C_n^X}_{2\to2}.
\]
Hence \(\norm{C_n^X}_{2\to2}^{1/n}\) has a limit equal to
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(X)\).

Fix \(n\) and \(0\le k\le n\).  Given a length-\(k\) self-avoiding path in
\(G\), a length-\(n-k\) self-avoiding path in \(H\), and a choice of the \(k\)
times at which to advance in the \(G\)-coordinate, we obtain a
self-avoiding path in \(G\square H\).  Indeed, if the product path visits the
same vertex twice, then both coordinate paths have the same coordinate index
at those two times; since the elapsed time is the sum of the two coordinate
indices, the two times are equal.  Therefore
\[
  C_n^{G\square H}
  \ge
  \binom nk\, C_k^G\otimes C_{n-k}^H
\]
entrywise.  Since the kernels are nonnegative, this implies
\[
  \norm{C_n^{G\square H}}_{2\to2}
  \ge
  \binom nk\,\norm{C_k^G}_{2\to2}\norm{C_{n-k}^H}_{2\to2}.
\]
Let \(k/n\to\alpha\).  Taking \(n\)th roots gives
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G\square H)
  \ge
  \exp\{h(\alpha)\}
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)^\alpha
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(H)^{1-\alpha},
\]
where \(h(\alpha)=-\alpha\log\alpha-(1-\alpha)\log(1-\alpha)\).  Maximizing
over \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) yields the claimed sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Product stress test for Route A7]
\label{cor:product-saw-stress}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree with \(d\ge3\), and let \(H\) be a
connected transitive amenable graph of bounded degree.  Then
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square H)
  \ge
  \sqrt{d-1}+\mu(H).
\]
Consequently, the SAW operator gap criterion can prove
\(\pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H)\) only if
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)
  <
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{d-1}+\mu(H)}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound combines Proposition~\ref{prop:product-saw-lower}, the tree
calculation \(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d)=\sqrt{d-1}\), and
Proposition~\ref{prop:amenable-saw-gap-fails}.  On the tree this calculation
is the same spherical-operator estimate used in
Proposition~\ref{prop:killed-tree}, since \(C_n=R_n\).  The final displayed
inequality is just the necessary condition
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square H)<1/\pc(T_d\square H)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This does not rule out Route A7 on products.  It shows what the route would
have to beat: mixed self-avoiding paths contribute at least additively to the
\(\ell^2\) SAW growth exponent.  If the displayed necessary inequality fails
for a product class, the boundary-energy or scattering routes must be used
instead of the global SAW operator gap.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Coarse high-branching product theorem]
\label{prop:high-branching-product}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(q=d-1\), and let \(H\) be a
connected bounded-degree graph with adjacency operator \(A_H\).  If
\[
  2\sqrt q+\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}<q,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H).
\]
In particular, it is enough that
\[
  2\sqrt{d-1}+\Delta_H<d-1,
\]
where \(\Delta_H\) is the maximum degree of \(H\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(A_T\) be the adjacency operator of \(T_d\), and let \(A\) be the
adjacency operator of \(T_d\square H\).  Then
\[
  A=A_T\otimes I+I\otimes A_H
\]
and \(\norm{A_T}_{2\to2}=2\sqrt q\).  Every self-avoiding path is a walk, so
the SAW kernel is entrywise dominated by the walk kernel:
\[
  C_n^{T_d\square H}\le A^n.
\]
Positivity gives
\[
  \norm{C_n^{T_d\square H}}_{2\to2}
  \le
  \norm{A^n}_{2\to2}
  \le
  \left(2\sqrt q+\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}\right)^n.
\]
Thus
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square H)
  \le
  2\sqrt q+\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}.
\]
The graph \(T_d\square H\) contains a copy of \(T_d\), so
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)\le \pc(T_d)=1/q.
\]
Under the displayed hypothesis,
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square H)<q\le1/\pc(T_d\square H).
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap} gives the claim.  The final sufficient
condition follows from \(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}\le\Delta_H\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This theorem is intentionally coarse and is not meant to compete with the
known product results.  Its role in this program is diagnostic: Route A7 is
not empty beyond regular trees, but its easiest proof only reaches product
graphs with sufficiently large tree branching.  Low-branching products such
as \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\) show why the SAW route is too crude; the line-factor
case is handled later by a direct \(p_{2\to2}=p_u\) argument.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-fiber high-branching tree bundles]
\label{prop:finite-fiber-high-branching}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(b=d-1\), and let \(F\) be a
finite set.  Let \(A_0\) be the adjacency matrix of a finite graph on \(F\),
and let \(P\) be a nonzero symmetric \(0\)-\(1\) matrix on \(F\).  Define a
graph \(G=G(T_d,F,A_0,P)\) on \(V(T_d)\times F\) by declaring
\((u,i)\) adjacent to \((u,j)\) when \(A_0(i,j)=1\), and \((u,i)\) adjacent to
\((v,j)\) when \(u\sim v\) in \(T_d\) and \(P(i,j)=1\).  Suppose that
\(G\) is connected and that \(P(i_0,i_0)=1\) for some \(i_0\in F\).  If
\[
  2\sqrt b\,\norm{P}_{2\to2}+\norm{A_0}_{2\to2}<b,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The adjacency operator of \(G\), under the identification
\(\ell^2(V(T_d)\times F)=\ell^2(V(T_d))\otimes\mathbb R^F\), is
\[
  A_G=A_{T_d}\otimes P+I\otimes A_0 .
\]
Since \(A_0\) and \(P\) are self-adjoint and
\(\norm{A_{T_d}}_{2\to2}=2\sqrt b\),
\[
  \norm{A_G}_{2\to2}
  \le
  2\sqrt b\,\norm{P}_{2\to2}+\norm{A_0}_{2\to2}
  < b.
\]
Every self-avoiding path is a walk, so if \(C_n\) is the length-\(n\)
self-avoiding path kernel on \(G\), then \(C_n\le A_G^n\) entrywise.  Hence
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)
  \le
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{A_G^n}_{2\to2}^{1/n}
  =
  \norm{A_G}_{2\to2}
  < b.
\]
The assumption \(P(i_0,i_0)=1\) gives a copy of \(T_d\) inside \(G\), namely
the vertices \(V(T_d)\times\{i_0\}\).  Therefore
\[
  \pc(G)\le \pc(T_d)=1/b,
\]
so \(b\le1/\pc(G)\).  The strict SAW operator gap
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(G)<1/\pc(G)\) follows, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[High-branching finite cyclic fibers]
\label{cor:finite-cyclic-fibers}
The graph \(T_d\square K_2\) satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square K_2)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square K_2)
\]
for every \(d\ge7\).  For every \(m\ge3\), the graph \(T_d\square C_m\)
satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square C_m)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square C_m)
\]
for every \(d\ge9\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For a Cartesian product with a finite factor \(H\),
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-fiber-high-branching} applies with \(P=I\) and
\(A_0=A_H\).
For \(K_2\), \(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}=1\), so the required inequality is
\[
  2\sqrt b+1<b,
\]
which holds for \(b\ge6\), i.e. \(d\ge7\).  For \(C_m\),
\(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}=2\), and
\[
  2\sqrt b+2<b
\]
holds for \(b\ge8\), i.e. \(d\ge9\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
These examples have genuine short cycles: \(T_d\square K_2\) contains a square
over every tree edge, and \(T_d\square C_m\) contains a cycle in every fibre.
The estimate is deliberately rough and high-branching, but it is a useful
cyclic calibration of the operator route.  It also allows finite-fibre
couplings that are not Cartesian products through the matrix \(P\).
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Nonbacktracking operator bound]
\label{lem:nb-operator-bound}
Let \(X\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph with adjacency operator
\(A_X\), and let \(N_n\) be the kernel counting length-\(n\) nonbacktracking
walks.  Put \(\rho=\norm{A_X}_{2\to2}\) and
\[
  \beta(D,\rho)
  =
  \begin{cases}
    \sqrt{D-1}, & \rho\le2\sqrt{D-1},\\[4pt]
    \dfrac{\rho+\sqrt{\rho^2-4(D-1)}}{2}, & \rho>2\sqrt{D-1}.
  \end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{N_n}_{2\to2}^{1/n}
  \le
  \beta(D,\rho).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The kernels \(N_n\) are polynomials in \(A_X\):
\[
  N_0=I,\qquad N_1=A_X,\qquad N_2=A_X^2-DI,
\]
and, for \(n\ge3\),
\[
  N_n=A_XN_{n-1}-(D-1)N_{n-2}.
\]
Indeed, \(A_XN_{n-1}\) counts all paths obtained by prepending one edge to a
nonbacktracking path of length \(n-1\).  The only bad paths immediately
backtrack across the prepended edge.  After deleting this two-edge backtrack,
one obtains a nonbacktracking path of length \(n-2\), and there are \(D-1\)
choices for the prepended neighbour, since it cannot be the first neighbour of
the remaining path.  The case \(n=2\) has \(D\) such choices, giving
\(N_2=A_X^2-DI\).
Thus \(N_n=P_n(A_X)\), where the scalar polynomials \(P_n\) satisfy the same
recurrence.  By the spectral theorem,
\[
  \norm{N_n}_{2\to2}\le \sup_{|\lambda|\le\rho}|P_n(\lambda)|.
\]
For fixed \(\lambda\), the recurrence has characteristic equation
\[
  r^2-\lambda r+(D-1)=0.
\]
If \(|\lambda|\le2\sqrt{D-1}\), both roots have modulus \(\sqrt{D-1}\), and
the possible double-root case gives only a polynomial factor in \(n\).  If
\(|\lambda|>2\sqrt{D-1}\), the larger root has modulus at most the second
branch in the definition of \(\beta(D,\rho)\).  Compactness of
\([-\rho,\rho]\) gives, for every \(\epsilon>0\), a constant \(C_\epsilon\)
such that
\[
  |P_n(\lambda)|\le C_\epsilon(\beta(D,\rho)+\epsilon)^n
  \qquad |\lambda|\le\rho,\ n\ge0.
\]
Taking \(n\)th roots and then \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Nonbacktracking product theorem]
\label{prop:nb-product}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(q=d-1\), and let \(H\) be an
finite or infinite connected \(\Delta\)-regular graph with adjacency operator
\(A_H\).  Set
\[
  D=d+\Delta,\qquad \rho=2\sqrt q+\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}.
\]
If
\[
  \beta(D,\rho)<q,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The graph \(T_d\square H\) is \(D\)-regular, and its adjacency operator is
\[
  A_{T_d}\otimes I+I\otimes A_H.
\]
Hence its adjacency norm is at most \(\rho\).  Every self-avoiding path is
nonbacktracking, so
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square H)
  \le
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{N_n}_{2\to2}^{1/n}
  \le
  \beta(D,\rho)
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:nb-operator-bound} and monotonicity of \(\beta(D,\cdot)\).
Since \(T_d\square H\) contains a copy of \(T_d\),
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)\le1/q.
\]
Thus \(\beta(D,\rho)<q\le1/\pc(T_d\square H)\), and
Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Nonbacktracking finite regular factors]
\label{cor:finite-regular-factor-nb}
Let \(H\) be a finite connected \(\Delta\)-regular graph, let \(T_d\) be the
\(d\)-regular tree, and put \(b=d-1\).  If
\[
  \beta(d+\Delta,2\sqrt b+\Delta)<b,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since \(H\) is finite, connected, and \(\Delta\)-regular,
\(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}=\Delta\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharper finite cyclic factors]
\label{cor:finite-cyclic-factors-nb}
The graph \(T_d\square K_2\) satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square K_2)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square K_2)
\]
for every \(d\ge5\).  For every \(m\ge3\), the graph \(T_d\square C_m\)
satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square C_m)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square C_m)
\]
for every \(d\ge7\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put \(b=d-1\).  For \(K_2\), \(\Delta=1\), so
\[
  D-1=b+1,\qquad \rho=2\sqrt b+1.
\]
If \(\rho\le2\sqrt{b+1}\), then
\[
  \beta(D,\rho)=\sqrt{b+1}<b
\]
for \(b\ge4\).  If \(\rho>2\sqrt{b+1}\), the larger root defining
\(\beta(D,\rho)\) is below \(b\) whenever
\[
  b>\rho/2
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  b^2-\rho b+(b+1)>0.
\]
For \(b\ge4\), the first inequality is immediate and the second is
\[
  b^2-(2\sqrt b+1)b+(b+1)
  =
  b^2-2b\sqrt b+1
  =
  b\sqrt b(\sqrt b-2)+1
  >0.
\]
Thus \(T_d\square K_2\) is covered for \(d\ge5\).

For \(C_m\), \(\Delta=2\), so
\[
  D-1=b+2,\qquad \rho=2\sqrt b+2.
\]
If \(\rho\le2\sqrt{b+2}\), then
\(\beta(D,\rho)=\sqrt{b+2}<b\) for \(b\ge6\).  In the remaining case, it is
enough to check
\[
  b>\rho/2
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  b^2-\rho b+(b+2)>0.
\]
For \(b\ge6\), the first inequality is immediate, and the second equals
\[
  b^2-(2\sqrt b+2)b+(b+2)
  =
  b^2-2b\sqrt b-b+2
  =
  b\bigl(b-2\sqrt b-1\bigr)+2
  >0.
\]
Thus \(T_d\square C_m\) is covered for every \(d\ge7\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A spectral-factor family]
\label{cor:spectral-factor-nb}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(s=\sqrt{d-1}\), and let \(H\) be
an infinite connected \(\Delta\)-regular bounded-degree graph.  Set
\[
  \alpha=\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}.
\]
If
\[
  s\ge 2+\max\{\sqrt\alpha,\Delta^{1/4}\},
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
It is enough to verify the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product}.
Put \(q=s^2\), \(D=d+\Delta\), and \(\rho=2s+\alpha\).  If
\(\rho\le2\sqrt{D-1}=2\sqrt{s^2+\Delta}\), then
\[
  \beta(D,\rho)=\sqrt{s^2+\Delta}<s^2
\]
because \(s\ge2+\Delta^{1/4}\) implies \(s^4>s^2+\Delta\).

It remains to consider \(\rho>2\sqrt{D-1}\).  The larger root in the
definition of \(\beta(D,\rho)\) is less than \(s^2\) if
\[
  s^2>\rho/2
\]
and
\[
  s^4-\rho s^2+(D-1)>0.
\]
The first inequality follows from \(s\ge2+\sqrt\alpha\).  For the second,
\[
  s^4-\rho s^2+(D-1)
  =
  s^2\bigl((s-1)^2-\alpha\bigr)+\Delta>0,
\]
again by \(s\ge2+\sqrt\alpha\).  Hence \(\beta(D,\rho)<s^2=q\), and
Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Regular amenable factors]
\label{cor:regular-amenable-factor}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(s=\sqrt{d-1}\), and let \(H\) be
an infinite connected amenable \(\Delta\)-regular graph.  If
\[
  s\ge 1+\sqrt{\Delta},
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square H)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since \(H\) is \(\Delta\)-regular, \(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}\le\Delta\).  Conversely,
if \(F_j\) is a Folner sequence and \(\partial_EF_j\) denotes the edge boundary,
then
\[
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_{F_j}}{A_H\mathbf 1_{F_j}}}{\norm{\mathbf 1_{F_j}}_2^2}
  =
  \Delta-\frac{|\partial_EF_j|}{|F_j|}
  \longrightarrow \Delta.
\]
Thus \(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}=\Delta\).  It remains to verify
Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product}.  Put \(a=\sqrt{\Delta}\).  Then
\[
  D=d+\Delta,\qquad D-1=s^2+\Delta,\qquad \rho=2s+\Delta.
\]
If \(\rho\le2\sqrt{D-1}\), then
\[
  \beta(D,\rho)=\sqrt{s^2+\Delta}<s^2,
\]
since \(s\ge1+a\) gives
\[
  s^4-s^2-\Delta
  \ge
  (1+a)^4-(1+a)^2-a^2
  =
  a(a^3+4a^2+4a+2)>0.
\]
If \(\rho>2\sqrt{D-1}\), the larger root defining \(\beta(D,\rho)\) is below
\(s^2\) once
\[
  s^2>\rho/2
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  s^4-\rho s^2+(D-1)>0.
\]
These follow from
\[
  s^2-\rho/2=s^2-s-\Delta/2
  \ge
  \frac{a(a+2)}{2}>0
\]
and
\[
  s^4-\rho s^2+(D-1)
  =
  s^2((s-1)^2-\Delta)+\Delta
  \ge
  \Delta>0.
\]
Thus \(\beta(D,\rho)<s^2=d-1\), and
Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Cluster-branching upper bound for tree products]
\label{prop:cluster-branching-pc}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, put \(q=d-1\), and let \(H\) be an
finite or infinite connected transitive graph.  For Bernoulli bond percolation
on \(H\) with parameter \(p\), let \(C_H(o)\) be the open cluster of a fixed
vertex \(o\in V(H)\), and define
\[
  \varphi_H(p)=\mathbb E_p\left[1-(1-p)^{|C_H(o)|}\right].
\]
If
\[
  q\varphi_H(p)>1,
\]
then \(p\ge\pc(T_d\square H)\).  Consequently, if the inequality holds at
some \(p_0\), then \(\pc(T_d\square H)<p_0\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Root \(T_d\), orient it away from the root, and keep any \(q\) root children
and the \(q\) forward neighbours at each non-root vertex.  Starting from a
fiber \(\{v\}\times H\), expose the open \(H\)-cluster of the current vertex
inside that fiber.  If this cluster has size \(M\), then a fixed forward
tree-neighbour fiber is reached whenever at least one of the \(M\) horizontal
edges leading to that neighbouring fiber is open.  Conditional on \(M\), this
has probability \(1-(1-p)^M\), independently for the \(q\) forward neighbours.

Let the offspring of a visited fiber be the number of forward neighbouring
fibers reached in this way.  Its mean is \(q\varphi_H(p)\).  When a
neighbouring fiber is reached, choose one open horizontal edge by a fixed rule
and then expose the \(H\)-cluster of its endpoint in the new fiber.  Future
clusters descended from distinct reached fibers lie in disjoint fibers, so the
successive generation sizes have the law of a Galton-Watson process with this
offspring distribution.  If the mean is larger than one, the process survives
with positive probability, producing an infinite open cluster in
\(T_d\square H\).  The strict statement follows from left-continuity of
\(\varphi_H\) at \(p_0\) under the standard monotone uniform coupling.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The quantity \(\varphi_H(p)\) cannot be replaced by a function of the
susceptibility \(\chi_H(p)=\mathbb E_p|C_H(o)|\) alone without additional tail
control.  Indeed, for a general positive integer-valued random variable \(M\)
with fixed mean \(\mu>1\), the expectation
\(\mathbb E[1-(1-p)^M]\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(p\) by putting most
of the mass at \(M=1\) and a vanishing amount of mass at a very large value.
Thus the cluster-branching criterion records a genuinely distributional input
from the factor \(H\), not just its susceptibility.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Cluster-sharpened finite cyclic factors]
\label{cor:cluster-sharpened-finite-cycles}
The graph \(T_d\square K_2\) satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square K_2)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square K_2)
\]
for every \(d\ge4\).  For every \(m\ge3\), the graph \(T_d\square C_m\)
satisfies
\[
  \pc(T_d\square C_m)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square C_m)
\]
for every \(d\ge5\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-cyclic-factors-nb} already proves the \(K_2\) claim
for \(d\ge5\), so it remains to treat \(T_4\square K_2\).  Put \(p_0=3/10\).
For \(K_2\), the fibre cluster size is \(M=1+X\), where
\(X\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(p_0\).  Hence
\[
  \varphi_{K_2}(p_0)
  =
  p_0+p_0^2-p_0^3
  =
  \frac{363}{1000},
\]
and
\[
  3\varphi_{K_2}(p_0)=\frac{1089}{1000}>1.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:cluster-branching-pc} gives
\(\pc(T_4\square K_2)<3/10\).

The graph \(T_4\square K_2\) is \(5\)-regular and has adjacency norm at most
\[
  \rho=2\sqrt3+1.
\]
For \(D=5\), the nonbacktracking exponent from
Lemma~\ref{lem:nb-operator-bound} is at most \(\beta(D,\rho)\).  We claim that
\(\beta(5,2\sqrt3+1)<10/3\).  Since \(10/3>\rho/2\), it is enough to check
\[
  \left(\frac{10}{3}\right)^2-\rho\frac{10}{3}+4>0.
\]
This inequality is
\[
  \frac{106}{9}-\frac{20}{3}\sqrt3>0,
\]
which follows by squaring from \(106>60\sqrt3\).  Therefore
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_4\square K_2)<10/3<1/\pc(T_4\square K_2)\), and
Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap} applies.

For cycles, Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-cyclic-factors-nb} already proves the
claim for \(d\ge7\).  It remains to treat \(d=5,6\).  For \(C_m\), let \(X\)
and \(Y\) be the indicators of the two fibre edges incident to the root.
Then \(M\ge1+X+Y\), and hence, for every \(p\),
\[
  \varphi_{C_m}(p)
  \ge
  1-(1-p)(1-p^2)^2 .
\]
At \(p_1=1/5\), this lower bound is \(821/3125\), so
\[
  4\varphi_{C_m}(p_1)\ge \frac{3284}{3125}>1.
\]
Thus \(\pc(T_5\square C_m)<1/5\).  On the operator side,
\(T_5\square C_m\) is \(7\)-regular with adjacency norm at most \(6\), and
\[
  \beta(7,6)=3+\sqrt3<5.
\]
The SAW operator criterion gives the result for \(d=5\).

For \(d=6\), take \(p_2=19/100\).  The same lower bound gives
\[
  5\varphi_{C_m}(p_2)
  \ge
  5\left[1-\frac{81}{100}\left(1-\frac{361}{10000}\right)^2\right]
  =
  \frac{12371319995}{10000000000}
  >1,
\]
so \(\pc(T_6\square C_m)<19/100\).  The graph is \(8\)-regular and has
adjacency norm at most \(2\sqrt5+2\).  Since \(100/19>(2\sqrt5+2)/2\), it is
enough to check
\[
  \left(\frac{100}{19}\right)^2
  -(2\sqrt5+2)\frac{100}{19}+7>0.
\]
The left hand side equals
\[
  \frac{8727}{361}-\frac{200}{19}\sqrt5>0,
\]
which follows by squaring from \(8727>3800\sqrt5\).  Hence
\(\beta(8,2\sqrt5+2)<100/19\), and the SAW operator criterion gives the
result for \(d=6\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The two-layer finite factor]
\label{cor:two-layer-factor}
For every \(d\ge3\),
\[
  \pc(T_d\square K_2)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square K_2).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:cluster-sharpened-finite-cycles} proves the claim for
\(d\ge4\).  It remains to treat \(T_3\square K_2\).

We first prove
\[
  \pc(T_3\square K_2)<\frac{39}{100}.
\]
Use the oriented tree-fibre exploration from
Proposition~\ref{prop:cluster-branching-pc}, but keep the reached subset of
the two-point fibre.  There are two symmetry classes of non-empty subsets:
singletons and doubletons.  At \(p=39/100\), the mean matrix for the two
forward child fibres is
\[
  M=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    2379/5000 & 1521/5000\\
    145119/250000 & 168831/250000
  \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Indeed, from a singleton, a fixed child is reached as a singleton with
probability \(p(1-p)\) and as a doubleton with probability \(p^2\).  From a
doubleton, a fixed child is reached as a singleton with probability
\(2p(1-p)^2\) and as a doubleton with probability \(3p^2-2p^3\).  The factor
two accounts for the two forward tree children.

With \(v=(1,7/4)^\mathsf T\), exact arithmetic gives
\[
  Mv=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    20163/20000\\
    1762293/1000000
  \end{pmatrix}
  >
  v
\]
coordinatewise.  Thus the finite-type Galton--Watson lower process is
supercritical, and
\[
  \pc(T_3\square K_2)<39/100.
\]

It remains to prove an \(\ell^2\) SAW operator bound below \(100/39\).  Let
\(C_n\) be the length-\(n\) self-avoiding endpoint kernel on \(T_3\square K_2\).
For \(n=15\), quotienting tree labels in the exact enumeration gives the
following coefficients for endpoints at tree distance \(r=0,\ldots,15\):
\[
\begin{gathered}
  192,\ 448,\ 592,\ 984,\ 1411,\ 1750,\ 1981,\ 2008,\\
  1837,\ 1498,\ 1073,\ 649,\ 301,\ 91,\ 15,\ 1 .
\end{gathered}
\]
The endpoint layer is determined by parity.  Combining these coefficients
with the \(T_3\) sphere-kernel norms, computed from
\[
  R_0=I,\qquad
  \norm{R_1}_{2\to2}=2\sqrt2,\qquad
  R_2=A_{T_3}^2-3I,\qquad
  R_{r+1}=A_{T_3}R_r-2R_{r-1}\quad (r\ge2),
\]
gives the exact bound
\[
  \norm{C_{15}}_{2\to2}
  \le
  639862+452048\sqrt2.
\]
Using \(\sqrt2<99/70\),
\[
  \norm{C_{15}}_{2\to2}
  <
  \frac{44771546}{35}
  <
  \left(\frac{100}{39}\right)^{15}.
\]
The kernels \(C_n\) are submultiplicative, so
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_3\square K_2)<\frac{100}{39}.
\]
Since \(\pc(T_3\square K_2)<39/100\), Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap}
applies.  The exact enumeration and arithmetic checks are reproduced by
\texttt{scripts/k2\_saw\_certificate.py}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Four-regular tree times finite cycles]
\label{cor:four-tree-finite-cycles}
For every \(m\ge3\),
\[
  \pc(T_4\square C_m)<p_{2\to2}(T_4\square C_m).
\]
Consequently, for every \(d\ge4\) and \(m\ge3\),
\[
  \pc(T_d\square C_m)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square C_m).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The second statement follows from the first and
Corollary~\ref{cor:cluster-sharpened-finite-cycles}, so it remains to prove
the \(d=4\) statement.  We split the cycle lengths into three cases.

First take \(m=3\).  At \(p_3=6/25\), the exact cycle-cluster distribution in
Proposition~\ref{prop:cluster-branching-pc} gives
\[
  3\varphi_{C_3}(p_3)=\frac{246948714}{244140625}>1,
\]
so \(\pc(T_4\square C_3)<6/25\).  A length-\(11\) exact self-avoiding
enumeration gives
\[
  \norm{C_{11}}_{2\to2}
  \le
  2649944+1532806\sqrt3.
\]
Using \(\sqrt3<97/56\), this is less than \((25/6)^{11}\).  Hence
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_4\square C_3)<25/6<1/\pc(T_4\square C_3)\).

For \(m=4\), take \(p_4=19/80\).  Exact cycle-cluster arithmetic gives
\[
  3\varphi_{C_4}(p_4)
  =
  \frac{1699239015678489}{1677721600000000}
  >1,
\]
and therefore \(\pc(T_4\square C_4)<19/80\).  The corresponding length-\(11\)
SAW certificate is
\[
  \norm{C_{11}}_{2\to2}
  \le
  3554176+2043694\sqrt3
  <
  \left(\frac{80}{19}\right)^{11},
\]
again using \(\sqrt3<97/56\).

Finally suppose \(m\ge5\), and put \(p_5=47/200\).  For \(m=5,6\), exact
cycle-cluster arithmetic gives
\[
  3\varphi_{C_m}(p_5)>1.
\]
For \(m\ge7\), expose only the first three fibre edges in each direction from
the root.  If \(L\) and \(R\) are the corresponding truncated open runs, then
\[
  \varphi_{C_m}(p_5)
  \ge
  \mathbb E\bigl[1-(1-p_5)^{1+L+R}\bigr],
\]
and exact arithmetic gives
\[
  3\mathbb E\bigl[1-(1-p_5)^{1+L+R}\bigr]
  =
  \frac{820807081028596686079073688981}
       {819200000000000000000000000000}
  >1.
\]
Thus \(\pc(T_4\square C_m)<47/200\) for every \(m\ge5\).

The length-\(11\) SAW enumeration is uniformly bounded for all \(m\ge5\) by
the radius-coefficient vector
\[
\begin{gathered}
  141050,\ 120742,\ 92376,\ 61444,\ 36592,\ 19364,\\
  8918,\ 3442,\ 1018,\ 200,\ 22,\ 1 .
\end{gathered}
\]
For \(m=5,\ldots,12\) this is checked directly, and for \(m\ge13\) a
length-\(11\) path cannot identify two distinct vertices of the line cover
modulo \(m\).  Combining these coefficients with the \(T_4\) sphere-kernel
norms gives
\[
  \norm{C_{11}}_{2\to2}
  \le
  4074050+2347722\sqrt3
  <
  \left(\frac{200}{47}\right)^{11}.
\]
The SAW operator criterion applies in all three cases.  The exact quotient
enumeration and arithmetic checks are reproduced by
\texttt{scripts/cycle\_saw\_certificate.py}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A vertical-cluster bound for \(T_d\square\mathbb Z\)]
\label{lem:vertical-cluster-pc}
Let \(d\ge3\), put \(q=d-1\), and define
\[
  \psi(p)
  =
  1-\frac{(1-p)^3}{(1-p+p^2)^2}
  =
  \frac{p(p^3-p^2+1)}{(p^2-p+1)^2}.
\]
If
\[
  q\psi(p)>1,
\]
then \(p\ge\pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)\).  Consequently, if the inequality holds
at some \(p_0\), then it holds on an interval below \(p_0\) and
\(\pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<p_0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(M\) be the size of the open cluster of the origin in one-dimensional
bond percolation on \(\mathbb Z\) with parameter \(p\).  It remains only to
compute \(\varphi_{\mathbb Z}(p)\) in
Proposition~\ref{prop:cluster-branching-pc}.
The one-dimensional cluster size satisfies
\[
  \mathbb P(M=m)=m(1-p)^2p^{m-1}\qquad m\ge1,
\]
and therefore
\[
  \mathbb E[t^M]
  =
  \frac{t(1-p)^2}{(1-pt)^2}.
\]
Taking \(t=1-p\) gives
\[
  \mathbb E[1-(1-p)^M]
  =
  1-\frac{(1-p)^3}{(1-p+p^2)^2}
  =
  \psi(p).
\]
The claim follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:cluster-branching-pc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A two-step vertical-cluster bound]
\label{lem:two-step-vertical}
Let \(d\ge3\), put \(q=d-1\), \(b=1-p\), and
\[
  c=\frac{1-p}{1-p+p^2}.
\]
For \(k=0,1,2\), define
\[
  A_k(z)
  =
  \frac{(1+c^k)bz}{1-pbz}
  -
  \frac{c^k b^2z}{1-pb^2z},
\]
and
\[
  H(z)=A_2(z)+\frac{bA_1(z)^2}{1-bA_0(z)}.
\]
Finally put
\[
  \Phi(p)=1-b^2H'(p).
\]
If
\[
  q^2\Phi(p)>1,
\]
then \(p\ge\pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)\).  Consequently, if the inequality holds
at some \(p_0\), then \(\pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<p_0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We use the same oriented tree exploration as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical-cluster-pc}, but look two tree generations ahead.
Fix a parent vertex \(x\), a child \(y\), and a grandchild \(z\).  Suppose the
available vertical cluster in the \(x\)-fiber has length \(m\).  A connection
from \(x\) to \(z\) through \(y\) exists if some open vertical component in the
\(y\)-fiber has at least one open source edge from the \(x\)-fiber and at
least one open target edge to the \(z\)-fiber.

Consider a component whose intersection with the \(m\)-interval has length
\(\ell\).  If it touches \(k\in\{0,1,2\}\) endpoints of the interval, it has
\(k\) independent outside vertical tails.  For one such tail \(G\),
\[
  \mathbb E[b^G]=\sum_{j\ge0}(1-p)p^jb^j=\frac{b}{1-p+p^2}=c.
\]
Thus the probability that this component fails to have both a source and a
target is
\[
  f_k(\ell)
  =
  b^\ell+c^kb^\ell-c^kb^{2\ell}.
\]
The generating function for a component with \(k\) boundary tails, including
its internal open vertical edges, is therefore
\[
  A_k(z)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}p^{\ell-1}f_k(\ell)z^\ell.
\]
Between consecutive components inside the interval there is one closed
vertical edge, giving a factor \(b\).  Hence the generating function for the
failure probability of the whole \(m\)-interval is
\[
  H(z)=A_2(z)+bA_1(z)\frac{A_1(z)}{1-bA_0(z)}.
\]
Writing \(H(z)=\sum_{m\ge1}F_mz^m\), the averaged failure probability over the
one-dimensional parent cluster size distribution
\[
  \mathbb P(M=m)=mb^2p^{m-1}
\]
is \(b^2H'(p)\).  Thus \(\Phi(p)\) is the probability that a fixed grandchild
is reached through its fixed parent child.

For each current individual there are \(q^2\) forward grandchildren at tree
distance two.  Let the offspring count be the number of these grandchildren
reached by the two-step procedure above.  This offspring distribution has mean
\(q^2\Phi(p)\).  When a grandchild is reached, choose one open target edge and
only then expose the vertical cluster at its endpoint in the grandchild fiber;
future vertical clusters descended from distinct reached grandchildren lie in
disjoint fibers and have the same one-dimensional law as the initial cluster.
Thus the even-generation exploration is a Galton-Watson process.  If its mean
is larger than one, the process survives with positive probability.  The
strict statement again follows from continuity.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The line factor for \(d\ge4\)]
\label{prop:tdz-d4}
For every \(d\ge4\),
\[
  \pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square\mathbb Z).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First suppose \(d\ge5\).
Put \(q=d-1=s^2\).  For \(H=\mathbb Z\), the nonbacktracking exponent from
Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product} previously gave the sufficient condition
\[
  \beta(d+2,2\sqrt{d-1}+2)<d-1.
\]
Here we use the same nonbacktracking bound together with the better
critical-probability estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical-cluster-pc}.  The
exponent is
\[
  \beta_d
  =
  \beta(d+2,2s+2)
  =
  s+1+\sqrt{2s-1}.
\]
Let \(r=\sqrt{2s-1}\) and \(t=s+1+r=\beta_d\).  Since
\(\gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_d\square\mathbb Z)\le t\), it is enough to prove
\(\pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<1/t\).

Using the formula for \(\psi\) in Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical-cluster-pc} and the
identity \(r^2=2s-1\), a direct calculation gives
\[
  s^2\psi(1/t)-1
  =
  \frac{
    s(3s^3+4s^2-13s-6)r
    +(s+1)(s^4+7s^3-16s^2+s+1)
  }
  {(r^2+2rs+r+s^2+s+1)^2}.
\]
For \(d\ge5\), we have \(s\ge2\).  Writing \(u=s-2\), the two numerator
coefficients become
\[
  s(3s^3+4s^2-13s-6)
  =
  (u+2)(3u^3+22u^2+39u+8)>0
\]
and
\[
  (s+1)(s^4+7s^3-16s^2+s+1)
  =
  (u+3)(u^4+15u^3+50u^2+53u+11)>0.
\]
Thus \(s^2\psi(1/t)>1\).  By Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical-cluster-pc},
\[
  \pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<1/t.
\]
The SAW operator gap criterion, Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap}, now
gives the claim for \(d\ge5\).

It remains to handle \(d=4\).  In this case \(q=3\), and the nonbacktracking
bound gives
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_4\square\mathbb Z)
  \le
  \beta_4
  =
  \sqrt3+1+\sqrt{2\sqrt3-1}.
\]
Let \(p_0=23/100\).  From Lemma~\ref{lem:two-step-vertical}, direct rational
arithmetic gives
\[
  9\Phi(p_0)-1>\frac1{100}.
\]
Therefore \(\pc(T_4\square\mathbb Z)<p_0\).  On the other hand,
\[
  \sqrt3<\frac{26}{15},
  \qquad
  \sqrt{2\sqrt3-1}<\frac{11}{7},
\]
and hence
\[
  \beta_4<\frac{26}{15}+1+\frac{11}{7}
  =
  \frac{452}{105}
  <
  \frac{100}{23}
  =
  \frac1{p_0}.
\]
Thus
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_4\square\mathbb Z)
  <
  1/\pc(T_4\square\mathbb Z),
\]
and Proposition~\ref{prop:saw-operator-gap} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A fiber-summed tree criterion]
\label{prop:fiber-summed-tree}
Let \(H\) be a transitive graph and let \(d\ge3\).  Put \(b=d-1\), fix a
vertex \(x_n\) of \(T_d\) at distance \(n\) from a root \(o_T\), and define
\[
  I_n(p)=\sum_{y\in V(H)}
  \mathbb P_p\bigl((o_T,o_H)\leftrightarrow (x_n,y)\bigr).
\]
If \(I_0(p)<\infty\) and
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} I_n(p)^{1/n}<b^{-1/2},
\]
then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(T_d\square H)\).  In particular
\(p\le p_{2\to2}(T_d\square H)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\theta<b^{-1/2}\) and \(C<\infty\) such that
\(I_n(p)\le C\theta^n\) for every \(n\ge1\).  For \(n\ge0\), let \(R_n\) be
the radius-\(n\) sphere kernel on \(T_d\).  Let \(K_n\) be the part of \(T_p\)
that connects pairs whose tree coordinates are at distance \(n\).  We claim
that
\[
  \norm{K_n}_{2\to2}\le I_n(p)\norm{R_n}_{2\to2}.
\]
Indeed, for fixed tree vertices \(u,v\) with \(\operatorname{dist}_{T_d}(u,v)=n\), the
kernel on the \(H\)-fibres
\[
  B_{u,v}(a,c)
  =
  \mathbb P_p\bigl((u,a)\leftrightarrow(v,c)\bigr)
\]
has row sums equal to \(I_n(p)\).  By symmetry its column sums have the same
bound, and Schur's test gives \(\norm{B_{u,v}}_{2\to2}\le I_n(p)\).  For
\(f\in\ell^2(T_d\square H)\), put \(g(v)=\norm{f(v,\cdot)}_{\ell^2(H)}\).
Then
\[
  \norm{(K_nf)(u,\cdot)}_{\ell^2(H)}
  \le
  I_n(p)\sum_{v:\operatorname{dist}(u,v)=n}g(v)
  =
  I_n(p)(R_ng)(u).
\]
Taking the \(\ell^2(T_d)\)-norm proves the claim.

The tree sphere kernels satisfy
\[
  \norm{R_n}_{2\to2}\le C_d(n+1)b^{n/2}.
\]
Thus
\[
  \norm{T_p}_{2\to2}
  \le
  I_0(p)+C'\sum_{n\ge1}(n+1)(\theta\sqrt b)^n
  <\infty,
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A base-sphere fiber criterion]
\label{prop:base-sphere-fiber}
Let \(B\) be a connected graph and let \(G\) be a graph whose vertex set is
partitioned as
\[
  V(G)=\bigsqcup_{u\in V(B)}F_u .
\]
For \(n\ge0\), let \(S_n^B\) be the distance-\(n\) sphere kernel on \(B\),
\[
  S_n^B(u,v)=\mathbf 1\{\operatorname{dist}_B(u,v)=n\},
\]
and define
\[
  J_n(p)=
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_B(u,v)=n}
  \max\left\{
    \sup_{a\in F_u}\sum_{c\in F_v}\tau_p(a,c),
    \sup_{c\in F_v}\sum_{a\in F_u}\tau_p(a,c)
  \right\}.
\]
If
\[
  \sum_{n\ge0}J_n(p)\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}<\infty,
\]
then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V(G))\).  In particular
\(p\le p_{2\to2}(G)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(L_n\) be the part of \(T_p\) connecting pairs of vertices whose fiber
indices are at distance \(n\) in \(B\).  For fixed \(u,v\in V(B)\) with
\(\operatorname{dist}_B(u,v)=n\), the block
\[
  B_{u,v}(a,c)=\tau_p(a,c),
  \qquad a\in F_u,\ c\in F_v,
\]
has row and column sums at most \(J_n(p)\), so Schur's test gives
\[
  \norm{B_{u,v}}_{2\to2}\le J_n(p).
\]
For \(f\in\ell^2(V(G))\), put
\[
  g(u)=\norm{f\mathbf 1_{F_u}}_{\ell^2(F_u)}.
\]
Then
\[
  \norm{(L_nf)\mathbf 1_{F_u}}_{\ell^2(F_u)}
  \le
  J_n(p)\sum_{v:\operatorname{dist}_B(u,v)=n}g(v)
  =
  J_n(p)(S_n^Bg)(u).
\]
Taking \(\ell^2(V(B))\)-norms gives
\[
  \norm{L_n}_{2\to2}\le J_n(p)\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}.
\]
The assumed summability lets us sum the \(L_n\)'s in operator norm, yielding a
bounded operator dominating \(T_p\), and hence \(T_p\) itself is bounded.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Restricted-shell control of separator square mass]
\label{prop:restricted-shell-layer-square}
Use the notation of Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber}.  For
\(\Sigma\subseteq V(B)\), let \(M_\Sigma\) be multiplication by
\(\mathbf 1_\Sigma\) on \(\ell^2(V(B))\), and let
\[
  S_\Sigma=\bigcup_{u\in\Sigma}F_u .
\]
If
\[
  A_\Sigma(p):=
  \sum_{n\ge0}J_n(p)\norm{M_\Sigma S_n^B}_{2\to2}<\infty,
\]
then every finite \(K\subset V(G)\) satisfies
\[
  \sum_{z\in S_\Sigma}\bigl(T_p\mathbf 1_K(z)\bigr)^2
  \le
  A_\Sigma(p)^2 |K|.
\]
Consequently, for a family \(\{\Sigma_a:a\in\mathcal A_L\}\),
\[
  \min_{a\in\mathcal A_L}
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p|K|}
  \sum_{z\in S_{\Sigma_a}}\bigl(T_p\mathbf 1_K(z)\bigr)^2
  \le
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p}
  \min_{a\in\mathcal A_L}A_{\Sigma_a}(p)^2
\]
uniformly over finite \(K\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(L_n\) be the part of \(T_p\) connecting fibre indices at base distance
\(n\), as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber}.  For a
finite \(K\subset V(G)\), put
\[
  g(u)=\norm{\mathbf 1_{K\cap F_u}}_{\ell^2(F_u)} .
\]
Then \(\norm{g}_2^2=|K|\).  The block-Schur estimate from
Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber}, followed by restriction to the
target fibres above \(\Sigma\), gives
\[
  \norm{(L_n\mathbf 1_K)\mathbf 1_{S_\Sigma}}_2
  \le
  J_n(p)\norm{M_\Sigma S_n^B g}_2
  \le
  J_n(p)\norm{M_\Sigma S_n^B}_{2\to2}\norm{g}_2 .
\]
Summing over \(n\) and using the triangle inequality in \(\ell^2(S_\Sigma)\)
yields
\[
  \norm{(T_p\mathbf 1_K)\mathbf 1_{S_\Sigma}}_2
  \le
  A_\Sigma(p)|K|^{1/2},
\]
which is the first claim.  Dividing by \(\chiBar_p|K|\) and minimizing over
\(a\) gives the displayed consequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This proposition is weaker than a global \(L^2\) bound when
\(\sum_nJ_n(p)\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}<\infty\), but it is aimed at the separator
problem.  The base set \(\Sigma\) may be a sparse grid, a horospherical slab,
or another separator.  Thus one can try to prove the layer-square estimate by
showing that the restricted shell operators \(M_\Sigma S_n^B\) are smaller
than the full shell operators on the scales where the fibre masses \(J_n(p)\)
are large.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[A limitation of periodic tree-level restrictions]
\label{prop:periodic-tree-restriction-lower}
Let \(T_d\) be the \(d\)-regular tree, \(d\ge3\), rooted at \(o\), and put
\(q=d-1\).  Let \(R_n\) be the distance-\(n\) sphere kernel and, for
\(L\ge1\) and \(r\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\), let
\[
  S_r^{(L)}=\{x\in V(T_d):\operatorname{dist}(o,x)\equiv r\pmod L\}
\]
and let \(M_r^{(L)}\) be multiplication by \(\mathbf 1_{S_r^{(L)}}\).  Then
for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
  \norm{M_r^{(L)}R_n}_{2\to2}\ge q^{n/2}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose a non-root vertex \(y\) whose level satisfies
\[
  \operatorname{dist}(o,y)+n\equiv r\pmod L .
\]
The \(q^n\) descendants of \(y\) at distance \(n\) from \(y\) all belong to
\(S_r^{(L)}\).  Hence
\[
  M_r^{(L)}R_n\mathbf 1_{\{y\}}
\]
is equal to \(1\) on these \(q^n\) descendants.  Since
\(\norm{\mathbf 1_{\{y\}}}_2=1\), the claimed lower bound follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Together with the tree sphere bound
\(\norm{R_n}_{2\to2}\le C_d(n+1)q^{n/2}\), this shows that periodic
tree-level restrictions can remove at most the Haagerup polynomial factor in
an operator-norm estimate.  They do not give a density factor tending to zero
with \(L\).  Thus the restricted-shell route cannot rely on sparsity of the
separator alone; it must also use the finite test set, averaging over shifts,
or a genuinely percolative backscattering estimate for the fibre masses.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Exponential base-sphere test]
\label{cor:base-sphere-exponential}
With the notation of Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber}, suppose that
there is \(\rho>0\) such that
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}^{1/n}\le \rho
\]
and
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}J_n(p)^{1/n}<\rho^{-1}.
\]
Then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V(G))\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\theta\) with
\[
  \limsup_n J_n(p)^{1/n}<\theta<\rho^{-1}.
\]
After increasing constants, \(J_n(p)\le C\theta^n\), while for every
\(\rho'>\rho\) with \(\theta\rho'<1\), we have
\(\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}\le C'(\rho')^n\).  Thus the summability hypothesis of
Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber} holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A pointwise shell-decay criterion]
\label{cor:pointwise-shell-decay}
Let \(G\) be a connected graph, and let \(S_n^G\) be its distance-\(n\) sphere
kernel.  Define
\[
  \tau_p^{\max}(n)=
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}\tau_p(x,y).
\]
If
\[
  \sum_{n\ge0}\tau_p^{\max}(n)\norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}<\infty,
\]
then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V(G))\).  In particular
\(p\le p_{2\to2}(G)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber} with \(B=G\) and singleton
fibres \(F_x=\{x\}\).  Then \(J_n(p)=\tau_p^{\max}(n)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bounded-fiber pointwise decay]
\label{cor:bounded-fiber-pointwise}
With the notation of Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber}, suppose that
\[
  \sup_{u\in V(B)}|F_u|\le M<\infty
\]
and define
\[
  \tau_{p,\mathrm{fib}}^{\max}(n)=
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_B(u,v)=n}
  \sup_{\substack{a\in F_u\\ c\in F_v}}\tau_p(a,c).
\]
If
\[
  \sum_{n\ge0}\tau_{p,\mathrm{fib}}^{\max}(n)\norm{S_n^B}_{2\to2}<\infty,
\]
then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V(G))\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For each pair of fibres at base distance \(n\), all row and column sums between
the two fibres are at most \(M\tau_{p,\mathrm{fib}}^{\max}(n)\).  Hence
\[
  J_n(p)\le M\tau_{p,\mathrm{fib}}^{\max}(n),
\]
and Proposition~\ref{prop:base-sphere-fiber} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[\texorpdfstring{\(L^2\)}{L2}-boundedness is open from the right]
\label{prop:l2-open-right}
Let \(G\) have maximum degree at most \(\Delta<\infty\).  If \(T_{p_0}\) is
bounded on \(\ell^2(V)\) for some \(p_0<1\), then \(T_q\) is bounded on
\(\ell^2(V)\) for every \(q\in[p_0,1]\) such that
\[
  q<p_0+\frac{1}{\Delta\norm{T_{p_0}}_{2\to2}}.
\]
Consequently, if \(p_c(G)<1\) and \(T_{\pc}\) is bounded, then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First work in a finite induced subgraph \(W\subset V\).  Let \(T_p^W\) be the
two-point matrix for percolation restricted to \(W\), and let \(A_W\) be the
adjacency matrix of \(W\).  Russo's formula and the BK inequality give, entrywise,
\[
  \frac{d}{dp}T_p^W(x,y)
  \le
  (T_p^W A_W T_p^W)(x,y).
\]
Indeed, if an edge \(uv\) is pivotal for \(x\leftrightarrow y\), then either
\(\{x\leftrightarrow u\}\) and \(\{v\leftrightarrow y\}\), or
\(\{x\leftrightarrow v\}\) and \(\{u\leftrightarrow y\}\), occur disjointly.
Summing over oriented edges gives the displayed inequality.

Put \(\lambda_W(p)=\norm{T_p^W}_{2\to2}\).  Integrating the differential
inequality and using positivity gives
\[
  \lambda_W(q)
  \le
  \lambda_W(p_0)+
  \int_{p_0}^q\norm{T_s^W A_W T_s^W}_{2\to2}\,ds
  \le
  \lambda_W(p_0)+
  \Delta\int_{p_0}^q\lambda_W(s)^2\,ds .
\]
Since \(T_{p_0}^W\le T_{p_0}\) as positive kernels,
\(\lambda_W(p_0)\le M:=\norm{T_{p_0}}_{2\to2}\).  The scalar comparison
inequality yields
\[
  \lambda_W(q)\le \frac{M}{1-\Delta M(q-p_0)}
\]
whenever the denominator is positive.

Let \(W\) increase to \(V\).  For finitely supported \(f\), the quadratic forms
\(\langle f,T_q^Wf\rangle\) increase to \(\langle f,T_qf\rangle\), while the
right-hand bound is uniform in \(W\).  Hence \(T_q\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V)\)
with the same bound.  Taking \(p_0=\pc\) gives the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Critical shell decay gives a strict gap]
\label{cor:critical-shell-strict}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree and \(p_c(G)<1\).  If
\[
  \sum_{n\ge0}\tau_{\pc}^{\max}(n)\norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}<\infty,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:pointwise-shell-decay} gives boundedness of \(T_{\pc}\).
Proposition~\ref{prop:l2-open-right} then gives boundedness of \(T_q\) for
some \(q>\pc\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Critical shell exponent criterion]
\label{cor:critical-shell-exponent}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree and \(p_c(G)<1\).  Define
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}^{1/n}
\]
and
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\tau_{\pc}^{\max}(n)^{1/n}.
\]
If
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\alpha\) and \(\rho\) such that
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)<\alpha,\qquad
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<\rho,\qquad
  \alpha\rho<1.
\]
By the definitions of the two limsups, after increasing constants if
necessary,
\[
  \tau_{\pc}^{\max}(n)\le C\alpha^n
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}\le C'\rho^n
\]
for every \(n\ge0\).  Hence
\[
  \sum_{n\ge0}\tau_{\pc}^{\max}(n)\norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}
  \le
  CC'\sum_{n\ge0}(\alpha\rho)^n
  <\infty.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:critical-shell-strict} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
For the \(d\)-regular tree, \(d\ge3\), one has
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_d)=\sqrt{d-1}\) and
\(\alpha_c^{\max}(T_d)=\pc(T_d)=1/(d-1)\).  Thus
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(T_d)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_d)
  =
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{d-1}}
  <1,
\]
recovering the strict \(L^2\) gap in this model from the critical shell
criterion.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Endpoint SAW shell criterion]
\label{cor:endpoint-saw-shell}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  For \(n\ge0\), define
\[
  U_n^{\mathrm{SAW}}(p)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{m\ge n}p^m C_m(x,y),
\]
where \(C_m\) is the length-\(m\) self-avoiding-walk endpoint kernel.  Put
\[
  \beta_c^{\mathrm{SAW,end}}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
  \bigl(U_n^{\mathrm{SAW}}(\pc)\bigr)^{1/n}.
\]
If
\[
  \beta_c^{\mathrm{SAW,end}}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If \(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\) and \(x\) is connected to \(y\), then the
open cluster connecting them contains an open self-avoiding path from \(x\) to
\(y\) of some length \(m\ge n\).  The union bound therefore gives
\[
  \tau_{\pc}(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{m\ge n}\pc^m C_m(x,y)
  \le
  U_n^{\mathrm{SAW}}(\pc).
\]
Hence
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)\le \beta_c^{\mathrm{SAW,end}}(G).
\]
The claim follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:critical-shell-exponent}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is a deliberately shell-resolved SAW condition.  It only counts
self-avoiding witnesses between two fixed vertices at distance \(n\), rather
than the full \(\ell^2\) operator norm of all length-\(m\) SAW endpoints.  On
the \(d\)-regular tree, the only self-avoiding path between two vertices is the
geodesic, so \(U_n^{\mathrm{SAW}}(\pc)=\pc^n\) and
\(\beta_c^{\mathrm{SAW,end}}(T_d)=1/(d-1)\).
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Excess-length endpoint SAW criterion]
\label{cor:excess-length-saw}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  For \(n,k\ge0\), define
\[
  E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{SAW}}(G)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n} C_{n+k}(x,y).
\]
Suppose that there are constants \(A<\infty\), \(a<\infty\), and
\(r<\infty\) such that
\[
  E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{SAW}}(G)\le A a^n r^k
  \qquad\text{for every } n,k\ge0,
\]
and
\[
  \pc(G)r<1
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \pc(G)a\,\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1.
\]
Then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Writing \(m=n+k\), the endpoint shell sum satisfies
\[
  U_n^{\mathrm{SAW}}(\pc)
  \le
  \sum_{k\ge0}\pc^{n+k}E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{SAW}}(G)
  \le
  A(\pc a)^n\sum_{k\ge0}(\pc r)^k.
\]
Since \(\pc r<1\), this gives
\[
  \beta_c^{\mathrm{SAW,end}}(G)\le \pc(G)a.
\]
The second displayed assumption and Corollary~\ref{cor:endpoint-saw-shell}
complete the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Excess-length nonbacktracking criterion]
\label{cor:excess-length-nb}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Let \(N_m(x,y)\) be the number of length-\(m\)
nonbacktracking walks from \(x\) to \(y\), and define
\[
  E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{NB}}(G)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n} N_{n+k}(x,y).
\]
Suppose that there are constants \(A<\infty\), \(a<\infty\), and
\(r<\infty\) such that
\[
  E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{NB}}(G)\le A a^n r^k
  \qquad\text{for every } n,k\ge0,
\]
and
\[
  \pc(G)r<1
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \pc(G)a\,\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1.
\]
Then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every self-avoiding walk is nonbacktracking, so
\[
  E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{SAW}}(G)\le E_{n,k}^{\mathrm{NB}}(G)
  \qquad n,k\ge0.
\]
The claim follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:excess-length-saw}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Nonbacktracking detour generating function criterion]
\label{cor:nb-detour-generating}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Let \(N_m(x,y)\) be the number of length-\(m\)
nonbacktracking walks from \(x\) to \(y\).  For \(n\ge0\), define
\[
  V_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(p)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{k\ge0}p^k N_{n+k}(x,y),
\]
and put
\[
  \delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
  \bigl(V_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc)\bigr)^{1/n}.
\]
If
\[
  \pc(G)\,\delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If \(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\), then the self-avoiding witness bound and
the domination of self-avoiding walks by nonbacktracking walks give
\[
  \tau_{\pc}(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{k\ge0}\pc^{n+k}C_{n+k}(x,y)
  \le
  \pc^n V_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc).
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)
  \le
  \pc(G)\,\delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G).
\]
The claim follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:critical-shell-exponent}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bounded-degree finite-state detour certificate]
\label{cor:bounded-degree-detour-certificate}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Suppose that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\).  Let
\(N_m(x,y)\) be the number of length-\(m\) nonbacktracking walks from \(x\) to
\(y\), and suppose that there are a finite set \(\mathcal S\), a nonnegative
\(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix \(M\), and nonnegative vectors
\(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{k\ge0}q^k N_{n+k}(x,y)
  \le
  a^\mathsf{T}M^n b .
\]
If
\[
  q\,\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since \(q\ge\pc(G)\), the displayed certificate also bounds
\(V_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc)\).  For every \(\theta>\rho(M)\), finite-dimensional
linear algebra gives a constant \(C_\theta<\infty\) such that
\[
  a^\mathsf{T}M^n b\le C_\theta\theta^n
  \qquad n\ge0.
\]
Thus
\[
  \delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G)\le\rho(M).
\]
Because \(\pc(G)\le q\), the displayed strict inequality implies
\[
  \pc(G)\delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  q\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  <1.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-detour-generating} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the bounded-degree version of the later regular-graph bridge
certificate.  It uses raw nonbacktracking counts rather than nonbacktracking
transition probabilities, so no regularity assumption is needed.  The price is
that the finite-state computation must estimate the full \(q\)-weighted detour
series directly.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Collatz bounded-degree detour certificate]
\label{cor:collatz-bounded-degree-detour}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Suppose that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\), and let
\(R\ge\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)^2\).  Let \(N_m(x,y)\) be the number of
length-\(m\) nonbacktracking walks from \(x\) to \(y\), and suppose that there
