are a finite set \(\mathcal S\), a nonnegative \(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\)
matrix \(M\), and nonnegative vectors \(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such
that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{k\ge0}q^k N_{n+k}(x,y)
  \le
  a^\mathsf{T}M^n b .
\]
If there are \(\lambda>0\) and a vector \(v\in(0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such
that
\[
  Mv\le\lambda v
\]
coordinatewise and
\[
  (q\lambda)^2R<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The Collatz--Wielandt inequality gives \(\rho(M)\le\lambda\), and
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)\le\sqrt R\).  Therefore
\[
  q\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  q\lambda\sqrt R
  <1.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:bounded-degree-detour-certificate} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the exact-arithmetic form of the bounded-degree count-kernel
certificate.  It differs from the regular bridge certificate below only in the
normalizing factor: raw count kernels require \((q\lambda)^2R<1\), while the
regular bridge-probability version requires
\(\bigl(q(D-1)\lambda\bigr)^2R<1\).  The repository checker supports both
criteria as separate exact certificate modes.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Bounded-degree path-sum detour certificate]
\label{prop:bounded-degree-path-sum-detour}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree, with
\(p_c(G)<1\), and suppose that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\).  Let
\(\mathcal S\) be finite, let \(M\) be a nonnegative
\(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix, and let
\(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\).  Suppose that for every \(n\ge0\) and
every pair \(x,y\) with \(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\), there are
nonnegative vectors \(\mu_{x,y}\le a\) and \(h_{x,y}\le b\), and, for each
\(1\le r\le n\) and \(\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal S\), a countable set
\(\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)\) with weights
\(w_{r,x,y}:\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)\to[0,\infty)\).  Define
\[
  K_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)
  =
  \sum_{f\in\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)}w_{r,x,y}(f),
\]
and assume that these sums are finite and \(K_{r,x,y}\le M\) coordinatewise.

Assume moreover that every nonbacktracking walk \(\gamma\) from \(x\) to \(y\)
of length \(n+k\), \(k\ge0\), is assigned injectively to data
\[
  \sigma_0,f_1,\sigma_1,\ldots,f_n,\sigma_n
\]
with \(f_r\in\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma_{r-1},\sigma_r)\), where for \(n=0\)
the data is just \(\sigma_0\), and that
\[
  q^k
  \le
  \mu_{x,y}(\sigma_0)
  \prod_{r=1}^n w_{r,x,y}(f_r)
  h_{x,y}(\sigma_n).
\]
If
\[
  q\,\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For fixed \(x,y\) at distance \(n\), sum the displayed bound over all
nonbacktracking walks from \(x\) to \(y\) of all lengths \(n+k\), \(k\ge0\).
Injectivity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \sum_{k\ge0}q^kN_{n+k}(x,y)
  &\le
  \sum_{\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_n}
  \mu_{x,y}(\sigma_0)
  \prod_{r=1}^n K_{r,x,y}(\sigma_{r-1},\sigma_r)
  h_{x,y}(\sigma_n)\\
  &=
  \mu_{x,y}^{\mathsf T}K_{1,x,y}\cdots K_{n,x,y}h_{x,y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(n=0\), the product is interpreted as the identity.  Since all matrices
and vectors are nonnegative and \(K_{r,x,y}\le M\), \(\mu_{x,y}\le a\), and
\(h_{x,y}\le b\), the last expression is at most \(a^\mathsf{T}M^n b\).
Corollary~\ref{cor:bounded-degree-detour-certificate} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the raw-count analogue of the regular path-sum transfer certificate
below.  The graph-specific task is to encode each weighted detour by phases
whose transfer sums are uniformly dominated by \(M\).  No regularity or
transition-probability normalization is used.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Semiregular-tree calibration]
\label{ex:semiregular-tree-detour}
Let \(T_{a,b}\) be the infinite \((a,b)\)-semiregular tree, where vertices in
the two bipartition classes have degrees \(a\) and \(b\), and put
\[
  r=(a-1)(b-1)>1.
\]
Then
\[
  \pc(T_{a,b})=\frac1{\sqrt r},
  \qquad
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_{a,b})\le r^{1/4}.
\]
Consequently
\[
  \pc(T_{a,b})\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_{a,b})
  \le r^{-1/4}<1,
\]
and hence
\[
  \pc(T_{a,b})<p_{2\to2}(T_{a,b}).
\]
\end{example}

\begin{proof}
The critical probability is the standard two-type branching-process threshold:
after two generations the expected number of descendants is \(p^2r\), so
\(\pc(T_{a,b})=r^{-1/2}\).

For the spherical bound, use the standard two-type Schur estimate.  Fix a
root \(o\).  There are positive constants \(c_A,c_B\), depending only on
\(a,b\), such that
\[
  \phi(x)=c_{\operatorname{type}(x)}r^{-d(o,x)/4}
\]
satisfies the following bound uniformly in \(x\) and \(n\).  If
\(d(x,y)=n\) and \(z\) is the confluent point of \(x,y\) with respect to
\(o\), write \(j=d(x,z)\).  For each fixed \(j\), the number of possible
vertices \(y\) is bounded, up to a constant depending only on \(a,b\), by
\(r^{(n-j)/2}\), while
\[
  \frac{\phi(y)}{\phi(x)}
  \le C_{a,b} r^{-n/4+j/2}.
\]
Thus each value of \(j\) contributes at most \(C_{a,b}r^{n/4}\), and summing
over the at most \(n+1\) possible values of \(j\) gives
\[
  \sup_x\phi(x)^{-1}\sum_{d(x,y)=n}\phi(y)
  \le C_{a,b}(n+1)r^{n/4}.
\]
Since the sphere kernel \(S_n\) is symmetric, Schur's test gives
\(\norm{S_n}_{2\to2}\le C_{a,b}(n+1)r^{n/4}\), and hence
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_{a,b})\le r^{1/4}\).  The strict gap follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:bounded-degree-detour-certificate}, since for a tree
\[
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}(x,y)=n}\sum_{k\ge0}\pc^kN_{n+k}(x,y)=1
\]
for every \(n\ge0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
For the \((2,3)\)-semiregular tree, \(r=2\).  The repository contains the
rational exact certificate
\[
  q=\frac34,\qquad R=\frac32,\qquad M=(1),
\]
for which
\[
  (q\lambda)^2R=\frac{27}{32}<1.
\]
The checker verifies the Collatz inequality and the one-state tree detour
majorization; the bounds \(p_c\le3/4\) and
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}^2\le3/2\) are supplied by the calculation above.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-quotient tree calibration]
\label{prop:finite-quotient-tree-detour}
Let \(H\) be a finite connected graph, let \(T=\widetilde H\) be its universal
cover, and let \(\vec E(H)\) be the set of directed edges of \(H\).  Let \(B\)
be the directed nonbacktracking matrix
\[
  B_{e,f}
  =
  \mathbf 1\{\operatorname{head}(e)=\operatorname{tail}(f),\ f\ne \bar e\},
  \qquad e,f\in\vec E(H),
\]
where \(\bar e\) is \(e\) with the opposite orientation.  Suppose that \(B\)
is irreducible and has Perron--Frobenius radius \(\beta>1\).  Then
\[
  \pc(T)=\frac1\beta,
  \qquad
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T)\le \sqrt\beta,
\]
and consequently
\[
  \pc(T)<p_{2\to2}(T).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(u\in(0,\infty)^{\vec E(H)}\) satisfy \(Bu=\beta u\).  The equality
\(\pc(T)=\beta^{-1}\) is the standard multitype branching-process calculation:
starting from a directed lift of an edge of type \(e\), the open
nonbacktracking descendants have mean matrix \(pB\), so survival starts exactly
when \(p\beta>1\).

It remains to bound the spherical kernels.  Fix a root \(o\in V(T)\).  If
\(x\ne o\), let \(\epsilon_x\) be the last directed edge on the geodesic from
\(o\) to \(x\), oriented away from \(o\), and let
\(\operatorname{type}(\epsilon_x)\in\vec E(H)\) be its projection to \(H\).
Set
\[
  \phi(o)=1,\qquad
  \phi(x)=u_{\operatorname{type}(\epsilon_x)}\beta^{-d(o,x)/2}
  \quad (x\ne o).
\]
Since there are finitely many directed edge types, all constants below may
depend on \(H\) but not on \(x,y,n\).

For any vertex \(z\), any forbidden first step at \(z\), and any \(\ell\ge0\),
the sum of \(u_{\operatorname{type}(\epsilon_y)}\) over vertices \(y\) reached
by a length-\(\ell\) nonbacktracking path from \(z\) avoiding that first step is
at most \(C_H\beta^\ell\).  Indeed, for \(\ell\ge1\) this sum is bounded by a
finite sum of coordinates of \(B^{\ell-1}u=\beta^{\ell-1}u\), and \(\ell=0\)
is absorbed into the constant.

Fix \(x\) and \(n\).  For \(y\) with \(d(x,y)=n\), let \(z\) be the last common
vertex of the geodesics \([o,x]\) and \([o,y]\), put \(j=d(x,z)\), and
\(\ell=n-j=d(z,y)\).  For fixed \(j\), the vertex \(z\) is determined by \(x\).
The preceding weighted count gives
\[
  \sum_{\substack{d(x,y)=n\\ d(x,z)=j}}\frac{\phi(y)}{\phi(x)}
  \le
  C_H\beta^{(j-\ell)/2}\beta^\ell
  =
  C_H\beta^{n/2}.
\]
There are at most \(n+1\) possible values of \(j\), whence
\[
  \sup_x\phi(x)^{-1}\sum_{d(x,y)=n}\phi(y)
  \le C_H(n+1)\beta^{n/2}.
\]
The distance sphere kernel \(S_n\) is symmetric, so Schur's test yields
\[
  \norm{S_n}_{2\to2}\le C_H(n+1)\beta^{n/2}.
\]
Thus \(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T)\le\sqrt\beta\).

Finally, a nonbacktracking walk in a tree cannot revisit a vertex.  Hence, if
\(d(x,y)=n\), then \(N_n(x,y)=1\) and \(N_{n+k}(x,y)=0\) for every \(k>0\).
The bounded-degree detour certificate applies with \(M=(1)\), giving
\[
  \pc(T)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T)\le\beta^{-1/2}<1.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This proposition packages all finite-type tree calibrations in one place.  It
contains the regular and semiregular tree examples after choosing a finite
regular or biregular base graph.  The remaining obstruction in the main
problem is not finite type on trees, but controlling genuine detours created by
cycles in non-tree quasi-transitive graphs.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Nonbacktracking bridge-probability criterion]
\label{cor:nb-bridge-probability}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Let \((X_m)_{m\ge0}\) be nonbacktracking random walk started at
\(x\): the first step is uniform among the \(D\) neighbours of \(x\), and each
later step is uniform among the \(D-1\) choices that do not immediately return.
For \(s\ge0\), define
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{k\ge0}s^k\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_{n+k}=y),
  \qquad n\ge1,
\]
and put
\[
  \lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
  \bigl(B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc(G)(D-1))\bigr)^{1/n}.
\]
If
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(G)
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For \(m\ge1\),
\[
  N_m(x,y)=D(D-1)^{m-1}\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_m=y).
\]
Thus, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
  V_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc)
  =
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n}
  \sum_{k\ge0}\pc^kN_{n+k}(x,y)
  =
  \frac{D}{D-1}(D-1)^n
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(\pc(D-1)).
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \delta_c^{\mathrm{NB,end}}(G)
  \le
  (D-1)\lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(G).
\]
The claim follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-detour-generating}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Directed-edge spectral bridge bound]
\label{cor:directed-edge-spectral-bridge}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Let \(\vec E\) be the set of directed edges, and let
\(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}\) be the nonbacktracking transition operator on
\(\ell^2(\vec E)\),
\[
  (\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}F)(u,v)
  =
  \frac1{D-1}\sum_{\substack{w\sim v\\ w\ne u}}F(v,w).
\]
Put
\[
  \sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)
  =
  \limsup_{m\to\infty}
  \norm{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}^m}_{2\to2}^{1/m}.
\]
If
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)<1
\]
and
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(s_c=\pc(G)(D-1)\), and choose \(\theta>\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\) so
that \(s_c\theta<1\) and \(s_c\theta\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1\).  By the
definition of the limsup, there is \(C_\theta<\infty\) such that
\[
  \norm{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}^m}_{2\to2}\le C_\theta\theta^m
  \qquad m\ge0.
\]
For \(m\ge1\), write the first nonbacktracking edge as a uniform directed edge
leaving \(x\).  If \(\nu_x\) is this initial distribution and
\(\mathbf 1_y^{\mathrm{in}}\) is the indicator of directed edges ending at
\(y\), then
\[
  \mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_m=y)
  =
  \ip{\nu_x}{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}^{m-1}\mathbf 1_y^{\mathrm{in}}}.
\]
Since \(\norm{\nu_x}_2=D^{-1/2}\) and
\(\norm{\mathbf 1_y^{\mathrm{in}}}_2=D^{1/2}\), this gives
\[
  \mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_m=y)
  \le
  C_\theta\theta^{m-1}.
\]
Consequently, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s_c)
  \le
  C_\theta\theta^{n-1}\sum_{k\ge0}(s_c\theta)^k
  =
  \frac{C_\theta\theta^{n-1}}{1-s_c\theta}.
\]
Thus
\[
  \lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(G)\le\theta.
\]
Letting \(\theta\downarrow\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\), the second displayed
assumption and Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-bridge-probability} imply the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Spherical growth from nonbacktracking growth]
\label{prop:sphere-from-nb-growth}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\).  With
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\) as in
Corollary~\ref{cor:directed-edge-spectral-bridge},
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  (D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{NB}}=(D-1)\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}\) be the
unnormalized nonbacktracking transition operator on directed edges, and let
\(N_n(x,y)\) be the number of nonbacktracking walks of length \(n\) from \(x\)
to \(y\).  If \(x\) and \(y\) have distance \(n\), then every geodesic from
\(x\) to \(y\) is nonbacktracking, so
\[
  S_n^G(x,y)\le N_n(x,y)
  \qquad n\ge1.
\]
Since both kernels are nonnegative, this pointwise domination implies
\(\norm{S_n^G}_{2\to2}\le\norm{N_n}_{2\to2}\).

Write \(e^-\) and \(e^+\) for the tail and head of a directed edge \(e\).  Let
\(C:\ell^2(V)\to\ell^2(\vec E)\) be \(Cf(e)=f(e^+)\), and let
\(B:\ell^2(\vec E)\to\ell^2(V)\) be
\[
  Bh(x)=\sum_{e^- =x}h(e).
\]
Then \(N_n=B\mathcal A_{\mathrm{NB}}^{\,n-1}C\).  Moreover
\(\norm{C}_{2\to2}=\sqrt D\) and \(\norm{B}_{2\to2}\le\sqrt D\).  Hence
\[
  \norm{N_n}_{2\to2}
  \le
  D(D-1)^{n-1}
  \norm{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NB}}^{\,n-1}}_{2\to2}.
\]
Taking \(n\)-th roots and then the limsup gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Adjacency-spectrum square criterion]
\label{cor:adjacency-spectrum-square}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Let \(A\) be its adjacency operator on \(\ell^2(V)\), put
\(\rho_A=\norm{A}_{2\to2}\), and let \(\beta(D,\rho_A)\) be the
nonbacktracking root from Lemma~\ref{lem:nb-operator-bound}.  If
\[
  \pc(G)\beta(D,\rho_A)^2<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\theta>\beta(D,\rho_A)\) such that
\[
  \pc(G)\theta<1,
  \qquad
  \pc(G)\theta^2<1.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:nb-operator-bound}, after increasing a constant if needed,
\[
  \norm{N_m}_{2\to2}\le C_\theta\theta^m
  \qquad m\ge0.
\]
Since every self-avoiding walk is nonbacktracking, for
\(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\),
\[
  \tau_{\pc}(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{m\ge n}\pc(G)^m N_m(x,y)
  \le
  C_\theta\sum_{m\ge n}\bigl(\pc(G)\theta\bigr)^m
  \le
  C'_\theta\bigl(\pc(G)\theta\bigr)^n.
\]
Hence \(\alpha_c^{\max}(G)\le\pc(G)\theta\).  Also, as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:sphere-from-nb-growth}, \(S_n^G(x,y)\le N_n(x,y)\) for
vertices at distance \(n\), and therefore
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)\le\theta.
\]
It follows that
\[
  \alpha_c^{\max}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  \pc(G)\theta^2
  <1.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:critical-shell-exponent} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This criterion is intentionally rough.  For the \(D\)-regular tree,
\(\rho_A=2\sqrt{D-1}\), so \(\beta(D,\rho_A)=\sqrt{D-1}\) and
\(\pc(T_D)\beta(D,\rho_A)^2=1\).  Thus pure adjacency-spectrum control reaches
only the critical boundary in the model case, whereas the bridge-resolved
criterion has a strict factor.  The corollary is nevertheless a useful test:
any proof relying only on the adjacency spectral radius cannot be the final
general mechanism unless it improves this loss.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A global nonbacktracking square criterion]
\label{cor:global-nb-square}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  If
\[
  \pc(G)\bigl((D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\bigr)^2<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put \(a=(D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\).  Since \(\pc(G)<1\), the displayed
assumption implies \(\pc(G)a<1\): this is immediate if \(a\le1\), and follows
from \(\pc(G)a<1/a\) if \(a>1\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:sphere-from-nb-growth}
also gives
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\sigma_{\mathrm{NB},2}(G)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  \pc(G)a^2
  <1.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:directed-edge-spectral-bridge} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The square criterion is a useful diagnostic but is deliberately coarse.  On
regular trees it sits at the critical boundary rather than recovering the
strict \(L^2\) gap, whereas the bridge-resolved calibration in
Example~\ref{ex:regular-tree-bridge-calibration} does recover the gap.  This
is the reason the finite-state certificates above are aimed at bridge
probabilities, not only at the global directed-edge operator.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-state bridge certificate]
\label{prop:finite-state-bridge-certificate}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), with
\(p_c(G)<1\).  Put \(s_c=\pc(G)(D-1)\).  Suppose that there are a finite set
\(\mathcal S\), a nonnegative \(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix \(M\), and
nonnegative vectors \(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such that, for every
\(n\ge1\),
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s_c)\le a^\mathsf{T}M^n b .
\]
If
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
where \(\rho(M)\) is the spectral radius of \(M\), then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For every \(\theta>\rho(M)\), finite-dimensional Perron--Frobenius theory, or
equivalently the Jordan normal form, gives \(C_\theta<\infty\) such that
\[
  a^\mathsf{T}M^n b\le C_\theta\theta^n
  \qquad n\ge1.
\]
Thus
\[
  \lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(G)\le \rho(M).
\]
The claim follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-bridge-probability}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proposition is intended as a certificate format.  A radial decomposition,
automaton, or transfer matrix may overcount nonbacktracking bridges, but if
the overcount has finite-state growth rate \(\rho(M)\) satisfying the displayed
inequality, then it is already strong enough to imply the strict \(L^2\) gap.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Bridge certificate with an upper bound on \texorpdfstring{\(p_c\)}{pc}]
\label{cor:finite-state-upper-pc}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\).  Suppose
that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\).  Put \(s_q=q(D-1)\), and suppose
that there are a finite set \(\mathcal S\), a nonnegative
\(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix \(M\), and nonnegative vectors
\(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s_q)\le a^\mathsf{T}M^n b .
\]
If
\[
  q(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since \(B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s)\) is nondecreasing in \(s\) and
\(\pc(G)\le q\), the same matrix bound holds at
\(s_c=\pc(G)(D-1)\).  Moreover,
\[
  \pc(G)(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  \le
  q(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)
  <1.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-state-bridge-certificate} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This form is the one most likely to be useful computationally.  It does not
require knowing \(\pc(G)\) exactly: an independently proved upper bound
\(\pc(G)\le q\) and a finite-state bridge certificate at the larger parameter
\(q(D-1)\) suffice.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Nonhomogeneous block certificate]
\label{prop:nonhomogeneous-block-certificate}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), and suppose
that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\).  Put \(s_q=q(D-1)\).  Let
\(\mathcal S\) be finite, let \(M\) be a nonnegative
\(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix, and let
\(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\).  Suppose that for every \(n\ge1\) and
every pair \(x,y\) with \(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\), there are a
nonnegative row vector \(\mu_{x,y}\), a nonnegative column vector \(h_{x,y}\),
and nonnegative \(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrices
\[
  K_{1,x,y},\ldots,K_{n,x,y}
\]
such that
\[
  \mu_{x,y}\le a,\qquad h_{x,y}\le b,\qquad
  K_{r,x,y}\le M\quad(1\le r\le n)
\]
coordinatewise, and
\[
  \sum_{k\ge0}s_q^k\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_{n+k}=y)
  \le
  \mu_{x,y}^{\mathsf T}
  K_{1,x,y}K_{2,x,y}\cdots K_{n,x,y}
  h_{x,y}.
\]
If
\[
  q(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For nonnegative matrices, coordinatewise domination is preserved under
matrix multiplication.  Hence
\[
  K_{1,x,y}K_{2,x,y}\cdots K_{n,x,y}\le M^n
\]
coordinatewise.  Multiplying on the left and right by the dominated
nonnegative vectors gives
\[
  \sum_{k\ge0}s_q^k\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_{n+k}=y)
  \le
  a^{\mathsf T}M^n b .
\]
Taking the supremum over all pairs at distance \(n\) yields the hypothesis of
Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-state-upper-pc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proposition is the form expected from radial or first-descent
computations.  A graph-specific argument may produce level-dependent block
matrices \(K_{r,x,y}\) rather than one homogeneous transfer matrix.  It is
enough to dominate all of those blocks coordinatewise by a single finite
matrix \(M\), because the growth test only sees \(M^n\).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Path-sum transfer certificate]
\label{prop:path-sum-transfer-certificate}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\), and suppose
that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\).  Put \(s_q=q(D-1)\).  Let
\(\mathcal S\) be finite, let \(M\) be a nonnegative
\(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\) matrix, and let
\(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\).  Suppose that for every \(n\ge1\) and
every pair \(x,y\) with \(\operatorname{dist}_G(x,y)=n\), there are
nonnegative vectors \(\mu_{x,y}\le a\) and \(h_{x,y}\le b\), and, for each
\(1\le r\le n\) and \(\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal S\), a countable set
\(\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)\) with weights
\(w_{r,x,y}:\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)\to[0,\infty)\).  Define
\[
  K_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)
  =
  \sum_{f\in\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma,\tau)}w_{r,x,y}(f),
\]
and assume that these sums are finite and \(K_{r,x,y}\le M\) coordinatewise.

Assume moreover that every nonbacktracking trajectory \(\gamma\) from \(x\)
to \(y\) of length \(n+k\), \(k\ge0\), is assigned injectively to data
\[
  \sigma_0,f_1,\sigma_1,\ldots,f_n,\sigma_n
\]
with \(f_r\in\mathcal F_{r,x,y}(\sigma_{r-1},\sigma_r)\), and that
\[
  s_q^k\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(\gamma)
  \le
  \mu_{x,y}(\sigma_0)
  \prod_{r=1}^n w_{r,x,y}(f_r)
  h_{x,y}(\sigma_n).
\]
If
\[
  q(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Sum the displayed bound over all nonbacktracking trajectories from \(x\) to
\(y\) of all lengths \(n+k\), \(k\ge0\).  Since the assignment is injective,
the resulting sum is bounded by the sum over all state sequences and all phase
fragments:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \sum_{k\ge0}s_q^k\mathbb P_x^{\mathrm{NB}}(X_{n+k}=y)
  &\le
  \sum_{\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_n}
  \mu_{x,y}(\sigma_0)
  \prod_{r=1}^n K_{r,x,y}(\sigma_{r-1},\sigma_r)
  h_{x,y}(\sigma_n)\\
  &=
  \mu_{x,y}^{\mathsf T}
  K_{1,x,y}\cdots K_{n,x,y}
  h_{x,y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:nonhomogeneous-block-certificate} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This proposition spells out the computational obligation behind a radial or
automaton certificate.  The graph-specific part is the injective
phase-decomposition and the local phase-weight bounds.  Once those are proved,
the remaining growth comparison is finite-dimensional.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Collatz--Wielandt bridge certificate]
\label{cor:collatz-bridge-certificate}
Let \(G\) be an infinite connected \(D\)-regular graph, \(D\ge3\).  Suppose
that \(q\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\pc(G)\le q\), and let
\(R\ge\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)^2\).  Put \(s_q=q(D-1)\).  Suppose that there
are a finite set \(\mathcal S\), a nonnegative \(\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\)
matrix \(M\), and nonnegative vectors \(a,b\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such
that, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s_q)\le a^\mathsf{T}M^n b .
\]
If there are \(\lambda>0\) and a vector \(v\in(0,\infty)^{\mathcal S}\) such
that
\[
  Mv\le \lambda v
\]
coordinatewise and
\[
  \bigl(q(D-1)\lambda\bigr)^2R<1,
\]
then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The coordinatewise inequality \(Mv\le\lambda v\) with \(v>0\) implies
\(\rho(M)\le\lambda\) by the Collatz--Wielandt formula, or by applying the
inequality iteratively and comparing norms.  Since
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)\le\sqrt R\), the final displayed inequality gives
\[
  q(D-1)\rho(M)\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(G)<1.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-state-upper-pc} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is the exact-arithmetic form of the certificate.  The inequalities
\(Mv\le\lambda v\) and \(\bigl(q(D-1)\lambda\bigr)^2R<1\) can be checked using
rational arithmetic once \(q,\lambda,R,M,a,b\), and \(v\) are rational.  The
repository accompanying this working draft includes a small checker for this
algebraic part and for the dimensions and signs of the boundary vectors,
either certificate-by-certificate or for all JSON certificates in a directory;
the graph-specific bridge majorization remains a separate mathematical
certificate.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Regular-tree calibration]
\label{ex:regular-tree-bridge-calibration}
For the \(D\)-regular tree \(T_D\), \(D\ge3\),
\[
  \lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(T_D)=\frac1{D-1}.
\]
Indeed, if \(\operatorname{dist}_{T_D}(x,y)=n\), a nonbacktracking walk from
\(x\) can hit \(y\) only by following the unique geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\),
and it then hits \(y\) at time exactly \(n\).  Hence
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s)
  =
  \frac1{D(D-1)^{n-1}}
  \qquad n\ge1
\]
for every \(s\ge0\).  Since \(\pc(T_D)=1/(D-1)\) and
\(\rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_D)=\sqrt{D-1}\),
\[
  \pc(T_D)(D-1)\lambda_c^{\mathrm{NB,br}}(T_D)
  \rho_{\mathrm{sph},2}(T_D)
  =
  \frac1{\sqrt{D-1}}
  <1.
\]
Thus Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-bridge-probability} recovers the strict \(L^2\)
gap on regular trees.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}
The regular-tree certificate is also the one graph-specific majorization that
the repository checker verifies directly.  In the one-state certificate with
\(M=(1/(D-1))\), the bound
\[
  B_n^{\mathrm{NB}}(s)
  =
  \frac{1}{D(D-1)^{n-1}}
  \le
  \left(\frac1{D-1}\right)^n
\]
is checked exactly for all \(n\ge1\).  General radial or automaton
majorizations still have to supply their own mathematical proof.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}
This criterion is weaker than the preceding self-avoiding version but is often
easier to estimate, since nonbacktracking walk counts can be attacked through
recurrences, transfer matrices, or spherical decompositions.  Its usefulness
depends on retaining fixed-endpoint and excess-length information; a global
operator bound for all nonbacktracking endpoints is usually too coarse in
low-branching product examples.
The generating-function form in Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-detour-generating} is
slightly more flexible than a separable estimate \(A a^n r^k\): it only asks
for the \(p_c\)-weighted detour series after endpoints at distance \(n\) have
been fixed.
On regular graphs, Corollary~\ref{cor:nb-bridge-probability} rewrites the same
target as an exponentially small nonbacktracking bridge-probability estimate.
Corollary~\ref{cor:directed-edge-spectral-bridge} is a convenient sufficient
condition, but Example~\ref{ex:regular-tree-bridge-calibration} shows why the
real target should remain bridge-resolved rather than just globally spectral.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[A quotient-tree fiber criterion]
\label{prop:quotient-tree-fiber}
Let \(G\) be a graph whose vertex set is partitioned as
\[
  V(G)=\bigsqcup_{u\in V(T_d)}F_u
\]
with \(d\ge3\).  Put \(b=d-1\), and for \(n\ge0\) define
\[
  J_n(p)=
  \sup_{\operatorname{dist}_{T_d}(u,v)=n}
  \max\left\{
    \sup_{a\in F_u}\sum_{c\in F_v}\tau_p(a,c),
    \sup_{c\in F_v}\sum_{a\in F_u}\tau_p(a,c)
  \right\}.
\]
If \(J_0(p)<\infty\) and
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}J_n(p)^{1/n}<b^{-1/2},
\]
then \(T_p\) is bounded on \(\ell^2(V(G))\).  In particular
\(p\le p_{2\to2}(G)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\theta<b^{-1/2}\) and \(C<\infty\) such that
\(J_n(p)\le C\theta^n\) for every \(n\ge1\).  Let \(L_n\) be the part of
\(T_p\) connecting pairs of vertices whose fiber indices in \(T_d\) are at
tree distance \(n\).  For fixed \(u,v\in V(T_d)\) with
\(\operatorname{dist}_{T_d}(u,v)=n\), the block
\[
  B_{u,v}(a,c)=\tau_p(a,c),
  \qquad a\in F_u,\ c\in F_v,
\]
has row and column sums at most \(J_n(p)\).  Schur's test gives
\[
  \norm{B_{u,v}}_{2\to2}\le J_n(p).
\]
For \(f\in\ell^2(V(G))\), put
\[
  g(u)=\norm{f\mathbf 1_{F_u}}_{\ell^2(F_u)}.
\]
Then
\[
  \norm{(L_nf)\mathbf 1_{F_u}}_{\ell^2(F_u)}
  \le
  J_n(p)\sum_{v:\operatorname{dist}_{T_d}(u,v)=n}g(v).
\]
Taking the \(\ell^2(T_d)\)-norm and using the tree sphere kernel \(R_n\) gives
\[
  \norm{L_n}_{2\to2}\le J_n(p)\norm{R_n}_{2\to2}.
\]
Since \(\norm{R_n}_{2\to2}\le C_d(n+1)b^{n/2}\), we obtain
\[
  \norm{T_p}_{2\to2}
  \le
  J_0(p)+C'\sum_{n\ge1}(n+1)(\theta\sqrt b)^n
  <\infty .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The full line factor]
\label{prop:tdz-full-line}
For every \(d\ge3\),
\[
  \pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square\mathbb Z).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We first prove the sharper identity
\[
  p_{2\to2}(T_d\square\mathbb Z)=\pu(T_d\square\mathbb Z).
\]
Put \(b=d-1\).  Let \(x_n\) be a fixed vertex of \(T_d\) at tree distance
\(n\) from the root and write
\[
  I_n(p)
  =
  \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
  \mathbb P_p\bigl((o,0)\leftrightarrow (x_n,k)\bigr).
\]
Yamamoto proves that for every \(p<\pu\), the quantities \(I_n(p)\) are finite,
submultiplicative in \(n\), and satisfy
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty} I_n(p)^{1/n}=\alpha(p),
\]
where \(\alpha(p)\) is the fixed-direction connection exponent
\cite{Yamamoto2018Critical}.  The same work, using Schonmann's theorem and the
strict monotonicity of \(\alpha\) on \([0,\pu]\), gives
\[
  \alpha(p)<b^{-1/2}\qquad (p<\pu).
\]
Hence for every \(p<\pu\) there are \(\theta<b^{-1/2}\) and \(C<\infty\) such
that \(I_n(p)\le C\theta^n\) for all \(n\ge1\).
Yamamoto's estimate \(\beta(p)<1\) for vertical connections gives
\(I_0(p)<\infty\).  Therefore
Proposition~\ref{prop:fiber-summed-tree} gives \(p\le p_{2\to2}\) for every
\(p<\pu\), so
\(\pu\le p_{2\to2}\).  The reverse inequality \(p_{2\to2}\le\pu\) holds for
every transitive graph, hence equality follows.

Hutchcroft proved \(p_c(T_d\square\mathbb Z)<p_u(T_d\square\mathbb Z)\) for
all \(d\ge3\) \cite{Hutchcroft2020Nonunimodular}.  Combining this strict
inequality with \(p_{2\to2}=\pu\) proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Hutchcroft and Pan prove a stronger product theorem: if \(T\) is a regular tree
and \(H\) is an infinite amenable Cayley graph, then
\(p_{2\to2}(T\square H)=p_u(T\square H)\); they also prove the analogous
identity for the lamplighter graph over \(T\), together with equality with the
natural nonunimodular tilted thresholds \cite{HutchcroftPan2024Dimension}.
Proposition~\ref{prop:tdz-full-line} is included here as a transparent
line-factor stress test: Yamamoto's fixed-direction exponent supplies the
fiber-summed decay, and Proposition~\ref{prop:fiber-summed-tree} isolates the
elementary operator step that converts that decay into \(L^2\)-boundedness.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Finite-length SAW diagnostics for \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\)]
\label{rem:tdz-finite-length-saw}
Proposition~\ref{prop:tdz-full-line} bypasses the following finite-length SAW
bounds.  They are retained as diagnostics for what a purely SAW-based proof
would have to achieve.  Let \(C_m\) be the length-\(m\) SAW endpoint kernel
on \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\).  Since the kernels \(C_m\) are submultiplicative,
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_3\square\mathbb Z)
  \le
  \norm{C_m}_{2\to2}^{1/m}.
\]
For fixed \(m\), write \(a_{r,h}^{(m)}\) for the number of length-\(m\)
self-avoiding paths from the origin to a fixed vertex at tree distance \(r\)
and height \(h\).  Then
\[
  C_m=\sum_{r,h}a_{r,h}^{(m)}R_r\otimes S^h,
\]
where \(R_r\) is the radius-\(r\) sphere kernel on \(T_3\) and \(S\) is the
shift on \(\mathbb Z\).  At the edge of the tree spectrum,
\[
  \norm{R_0}=1,\qquad
  \norm{R_1}=2\sqrt2,\qquad
  \norm{R_2}=5,\qquad
  \norm{R_{r+1}}=2\sqrt2\,\norm{R_r}-2\norm{R_{r-1}}.
\]
The parity identity \(r+h\equiv m\pmod 2\) makes the triangle bound sharp at a
vertical frequency \(0\) or \(\pi\).  Exact enumeration gives
\[
  \norm{C_{12}}_{2\to2}
  =
  3110764+2209048\sqrt2,
\]
and hence
\[
  \norm{C_{12}}_{2\to2}^{1/12}\le3.683286.
\]
Similarly, the same finite computation gives
\[
  \norm{C_{13}}_{2\to2}^{1/13}\le3.669978,
  \qquad
  \norm{C_{14}}_{2\to2}^{1/14}\le3.657847.
\]
Quotienting out the tree labels in the exact enumeration reaches one further
step and gives
\[
  \norm{C_{15}}_{2\to2}
  =
  134618428+95108784\sqrt2,
  \qquad
  \norm{C_{15}}_{2\to2}^{1/15}\le3.647512.
\]
These improve the nonbacktracking exponent
\(\beta(5,2\sqrt2+2)\approx3.766408\), but are still much too large to combine
with the vertical-branching \(p_c\)-upper bounds above.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A finite-type interval bound for \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\)]
\label{rem:tdz-interval-branching}
The one- and two-step estimates above keep only one vertical cluster after each
tree move.  A slightly stronger oriented lower process keeps one contiguous
interval in each reached fiber.  Fix \(M\ge1\).  Type \(m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\)
means that the current fiber contains a reachable interval of length \(m\),
with \(m=M\) meaning length at least \(M\).  From a parent interval of length
\(m\), expose the horizontal edges from its \(m\) sites to a fixed child fiber
and then expose the vertical edges in that child fiber.  Retain the capped
length of the longest contiguous reached interval as the child type, or retain
no child if there is no open horizontal seed.  If \(P^{(M)}_{m\ell}(p)\) is the
single-child transition probability, then the mean matrix of this finite-type
Galton-Watson lower process on \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\) is
\[
  A^{(M)}_{m\ell}(p)=2P^{(M)}_{m\ell}(p).
\]
Thus \(\rho(A^{(M)}(p))>1\) implies \(p\ge\pc(T_3\square\mathbb Z)\), and by
continuity a strict inequality at \(p_0\) implies
\(\pc(T_3\square\mathbb Z)<p_0\).

For \(M=6\) and \(p_0=61/200\), exact enumeration gives a rational
Perron-Frobenius certificate.  With
\[
  v=(6271,11456,15785,19374,22333,24781),
\]
one has
\[
  \min_{1\le m\le6}
  \frac{(A^{(6)}(p_0)v)_m}{v_m}
  >
  1.00714.
\]
Consequently
\[
  \pc(T_3\square\mathbb Z)<\frac{61}{200}.
\]
The finite calculation only inspects horizontal seed subsets and vertical
edges in the window \([-(M-1),m-1+(M-1)]\), since reaching the boundary already
certifies capped type \(M\).  It is reproducible with
\texttt{scripts/interval\_branching\_bound.py}.  This improves the available
\(p_c\)-upper bound in the numerical route, but it would still need an operator
estimate
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_3\square\mathbb Z)<\frac{200}{61}\approx3.27869,
\]
whereas the current finite-length bound is \(3.647512\).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A decorated-strip bound for \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\)]
\label{rem:tdz-decorated-strip}
Yamamoto's characterization of the critical point of \(T_d\square\mathbb Z\)
by the fixed-direction connection exponent gives another way to improve the
\(p_c\)-upper side~\cite{Yamamoto2018Critical}.  Let \(x_n\) be a vertex of
\(T_3\) at distance \(n\) from a root \(o\), and define
\[
  \alpha(p)
  =
  \lim_{n\to\infty}
  \mathbb P_p\bigl((o,0)\leftrightarrow (x_n,0)\bigr)^{1/n}.
\]
For \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\), Yamamoto's criterion says that
\(\alpha(p)>1/2\) implies \(p>\pc(T_3\square\mathbb Z)\).

Consider the following finite decorated strip inside \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\).
Take the geodesic from \(o\) to \(x_n\), keep the twelve heights
\(\{-5,\ldots,6\}\), and attach at each internal geodesic fiber its one
off-geodesic side fiber, again restricted to these twelve heights.  After
integrating out the thirty-four edges in one decorated column, the transfer matrix
on the \(2^{12}-1=4095\) non-empty subsets of the geodesic fiber has entries in
\(\mathbb Q\) when \(p\in\mathbb Q\).  At
\[
  p_0=\frac{5863}{20000},
\]
exact integer arithmetic gives a Perron-Frobenius certificate
\[
  \min_A\frac{2(M(p_0)v)_A}{v_A}>1.000320
\]
for a positive integer vector \(v\in\mathbb Z^{4095}\).  Hence
\(\rho(M(p_0))>1/2\), so the restricted-strip connection probability already
has exponential rate larger than \(1/2\) for connection to at least one of the
twelve terminal heights.  Since this is a finite height set, FKG and the event
that the bounded vertical segment from that terminal height to height \(0\) is
open show that the same lower exponential rate applies to the fixed-height
connection defining \(\alpha\).  Therefore
\[
  \pc(T_3\square\mathbb Z)<\frac{5863}{20000}.
\]
The certificate is reproducible with
\texttt{scripts/decorated\_strip\_fixedp\_certificate.py}.  This is still not
enough for the current SAW criterion: it would require
\[
  \gamma_{\mathrm{SAW},2}(T_3\square\mathbb Z)
  <
  \frac{20000}{5863}
  \approx3.41122,
\]
while the best finite-length certificate above is \(3.647512\).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Further diagnostics for \(T_3\square\mathbb Z\)]
\label{rem:tdz-further-diagnostics}
Several stronger finite computations were tested after the decorated-strip
bound.  They are useful mostly because they identify which natural numerical
routes would not by themselves reprove Proposition~\ref{prop:tdz-full-line}.

First, one may improve the interval branching process by retaining an arbitrary
finite reached subset of a vertical fiber rather than only one interval.  With
type width \(W\), the type is a non-empty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,W\}\)
containing \(0\), normalized by vertical translation.  A child type is chosen
as a reached subset of span at most \(W\).  This one-step finite-subset lower
process gives substantially better non-oriented \(p_c\)-upper diagnostics than
the one-interval process:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
W&7&8&9&10\\
\hline
\text{threshold diagnostic}
&0.2963779&(0.2961,0.2962)&\approx0.2960&>0.29545.
\end{array}
\]
In particular, already at the older height-ten decorated-strip point
\(p=5909/20000\), the width \(10\) ratio is still only \(0.9975811\).  Thus
this retention rule is close to, but does not beat, the current height-twelve
decorated-strip certificate.

Second, depth-two tree-block explorations were tested.  A naive Monte Carlo
version looked promising, but it exposed vertical edges in both the incoming
and outgoing boundary fibers of a block; iterating such blocks would reuse
boundary-fiber randomness.  Valid regenerative variants, where the state
records either already-expanded sets or raw boundary seed sets, are much
weaker.  For type width \(7\) and margin \(2\), their ratios at \(p=0.296\)
are about \(0.956\), and they cross one only near \(p=0.301\).

Finally, on the operator side, local finite-memory self-avoidance was tested.
A memory-\(m\) walk is forbidden to step onto any of its previous \(m\)
vertices and hence contains all self-avoiding walks.  Row-sum growth is far too
large: even memory \(10\) has growth \(3.828133\).  Applying the same spherical
\(\ell^2\) endpoint evaluation used in Remark~\ref{rem:tdz-finite-length-saw}
is stronger, but still not enough.  For instance,
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
(m,n)&(4,16)&(6,16)&(8,14)\\
\hline
\|D_n^{(m)}\|_{2\to2}^{1/n}
&3.699474&3.664311&3.666224.
\end{array}
\]
These values remain above the exact finite-length SAW certificate
\(3.647512\), and far above the current target
\[
  \frac{20000}{5863}\approx3.41122.
\]
Thus these numerical routes would still require either a genuinely asymptotic
\(L^2\) self-avoidance estimate or the direct \(p_{2\to2}\) argument supplied
by Proposition~\ref{prop:tdz-full-line}.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A lattice-factor family]
\label{cor:tdzr-nb}
Let \(r\ge1\).  If
\[
  \sqrt{d-1}\ge2+\sqrt{2r},
\]
then
\[
  \pc(T_d\square\mathbb Z^r)<p_{2\to2}(T_d\square\mathbb Z^r).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put \(q=d-1\) and \(s=\sqrt q\).  For \(H=\mathbb Z^r\), we have
\(\Delta=2r\) and \(\norm{A_H}_{2\to2}=2r\).  The nonbacktracking criterion
therefore becomes
\[
  \beta(d+2r,2s+2r)<s^2.
\]
Since
\[
  2s+2r>2\sqrt{s^2+2r}=2\sqrt{d+2r-1},
\]
the second branch of \(\beta\) applies, and the condition is
\[
  s+r+\sqrt{r(2s+r-2)}<s^2.
\]
Let
\[
  F_r(s)=s^2-s-r-\sqrt{r(2s+r-2)}.
\]
For \(s\ge2+\sqrt{2r}\),
\[
  F'_r(s)=2s-1-\frac{\sqrt r}{\sqrt{2s+r-2}}>0,
\]
and
\[
  F_r(2+\sqrt{2r})
  =
  2+2\sqrt{2r}
  >0.
\]
Thus \(F_r(s)>0\), and Proposition~\ref{prop:nb-product} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Corollary~\ref{cor:tdzr-nb} is a deliberately crude family statement.  It is
useful here because it shows that the nonbacktracking SAW route handles
tree-times-lattice products in a uniform high-branching regime.  For \(r=1\),
Proposition~\ref{prop:tdz-d4} is sharper because it also uses a line-specific
upper bound on \(p_c\).  The real test for this route remains the
low-branching regime, where the threshold above is far from sharp.
\end{remark}

\section{A finite-set escape abstraction}

The following abstraction records a possible way to prove \eqref{eq:fe}.  It
is intentionally formulated independently of hyperbolicity or planarity.

\begin{definition}[Kernel leakage profile]
Let \(Q\) be a positive symmetric kernel on \(V\) satisfying
\[
  \sup_x\sum_yQ(x,y)\le1.
\]
For a finite non-empty set \(K\subset V\), define
\[
  \mathcal M_Q(K)=\frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q(x,y).
\]
For \(\delta>0\), say that \(K\) is \(\delta\)-leaky for \(Q\) if
\(\mathcal M_Q(K)\le\delta\).
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Uniform leakage implies finite-set escape]
\label{prop:uniform-leakage}
Let \(p_n\uparrow\pc\).  Suppose that for every \(\delta>0\) there is \(n_0\)
such that every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) is \(\delta\)-leaky for
\(Q_{p_n}\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\).  Then finite-set escape holds along
\(p_n\):
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_K\mathcal M_{Q_{p_n}}(K)=0.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
This is just the definition of the supremum.  Given \(\delta>0\), the
assumption says \(\mathcal M_{Q_{p_n}}(K)\le\delta\) for every finite non-empty
\(K\) and every sufficiently large \(n\).  Taking the supremum over \(K\) gives
\(\sup_K\mathcal M_{Q_{p_n}}(K)\le\delta\), and \(\delta\) was arbitrary.
\end{proof}

The proposition is tautological.  Its value is conceptual: to solve
Conjecture~\ref{conj:l2bs} via Theorem~\ref{thm:hutchcroft-criterion}, one must
prove uniform leakage for \(Q_p\) near \(\pc\).  Known proofs obtain such
leakage from special geometry.  The desired proof would derive it from
nonamenability.

\subsection{A separator version}

The next criterion is also elementary, but it is closer to known geometric
proofs.  It says that if every finite set can be decomposed into many pieces
whose \(Q_p\)-interaction is mostly external, then finite-set escape follows.

\begin{definition}[Scattering partition]
Let \(Q\) be as above.  A partition \(K=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_m\) of a finite set
is \((a,b)\)-scattering for \(Q\) if
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{x,y\in K_i}Q(x,y)\le a
\]
and
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{i\ne j}\sum_{x\in K_i,y\in K_j}Q(x,y)\le b.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Scattering criterion]
\label{prop:scattering}
If, for every \(\delta>0\), all sufficiently near-critical \(Q_p\) admit a
\((\delta,\delta)\)-scattering partition of every finite \(K\subset V\), then
finite-set escape holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For such a partition,
\[
  \mathcal M_{Q_p}(K)
  =
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_i\sum_{x,y\in K_i}Q_p(x,y)
  +
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{i\ne j}\sum_{x\in K_i,y\in K_j}Q_p(x,y)
  \le 2\delta.
\]
Since \(\delta\) is arbitrary, the supremum over finite \(K\) tends to zero.
\end{proof}

In the hyperbolic proof, the role of the partition is played by large-scale
half-space decompositions: most vertices see most other vertices far out in
one or two separated directions, and subcritical connectivity to such distant
regions is small after normalization.  A possible path to a new theorem is to
identify a weaker separator hypothesis implied by nonamenability alone, or by
a new group-theoretic condition not covered by existing results.

\subsection{A separator-convolution version}

The preceding scattering criterion is intentionally terse.  The next version
records the percolation input that a geometric separator can exploit.  It uses
BK to turn cross-piece connections into a two-point convolution through
separator sets.

Let
\[
  K=K_0\sqcup K_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup K_m
\]
be a buffered partition of a finite set, where \(K_0\) is the part we do not
try to separate.  For \(i,j\ge1\), \(i\ne j\), call a set
\(W_{ij}\subseteq V\) a proper path separator from \(K_i\) to \(K_j\) if
\[
  W_{ij}\cap(K_i\cup K_j)=\varnothing
\]
and every graph path from a vertex of \(K_i\) to a vertex of \(K_j\) visits
\(W_{ij}\).  Define, for \(i\ge1\),
\[
  U_i^p(z)=\sum_{x\in K_i}\tau_p(x,z)
\]
and
\[
  \mathcal C_p(K_1,\ldots,K_m;W)
  =
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p |K|}
  \sum_{i\ne j}\sum_{z\in W_{ij}}U_i^p(z)U_j^p(z).
\]
Also define the normalized buffer mass
\[
  \mathcal B_p(K_0;K)
  =
  \frac{2}{\chiBar_p |K|}
  \sum_{x\in K_0,y\in K}\tau_p(x,y).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Separator convolution controls cross mass]
\label{lem:separator-convolution}
With the notation above, the cross mass between the non-buffer pieces satisfies
\[
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p |K|}
  \sum_{\substack{i\ne j\\ i,j\ge1}}\sum_{x\in K_i,y\in K_j}\tau_p(x,y)
  \le
  \mathcal C_p(K_1,\ldots,K_m;W).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(i,j\ge1\), \(i\ne j\), \(x\in K_i\), and \(y\in K_j\).  If
\(x\leftrightarrow y\), then some open self-avoiding path from \(x\) to \(y\)
visits \(W_{ij}\).  Let \(z\) be the first vertex of \(W_{ij}\) on this path.
Since \(W_{ij}\) is disjoint from \(K_i\cup K_j\), \(z\) is not an endpoint.
The two path segments from \(x\) to \(z\) and from \(z\) to \(y\) are
edge-disjoint.  Thus the event \(\{x\leftrightarrow y\}\) is contained in
\[
  \bigcup_{z\in W_{ij}}
  \bigl(\{x\leftrightarrow z\}\circ\{z\leftrightarrow y\}\bigr),
\]
where \(\circ\) denotes disjoint occurrence.  The BK inequality gives
\[
  \tau_p(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{z\in W_{ij}}\tau_p(x,z)\tau_p(z,y).
\]
Summing over \(x,y,i,j\), and using symmetry of \(\tau_p\), gives the displayed
bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Separator-convolution criterion]
\label{prop:separator-convolution-criterion}
Suppose that for every \(\delta>0\) and all \(p\) sufficiently close to
\(\pc\), every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) admits a buffered partition
\[
  K=K_0\sqcup K_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup K_m
\]
and proper path separators \(W_{ij}\), \(i,j\ge1\), \(i\ne j\), such that
\[
  \mathcal B_p(K_0;K)\le\delta,
\]
\[
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p |K|}
  \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{x,y\in K_i}\tau_p(x,y)
  \le\delta
\]
and
\[
  \mathcal C_p(K_1,\ldots,K_m;W)\le\delta .
\]
Then finite-set escape holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The mass of pairs with at least one endpoint in \(K_0\) is bounded above by
\(\mathcal B_p(K_0;K)\le\delta\).  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:separator-convolution}, the normalized cross-piece mass among
the non-buffer pieces is at most \(\delta\).  The normalized same-piece mass is
at most \(\delta\) by assumption, so
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)\le3\delta
\]
for every finite non-empty \(K\), once \(p\) is sufficiently close to
\(\pc\).  Since \(\delta\) is arbitrary, the supremum over \(K\) tends to zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This criterion is still conditional, but it separates the two tasks in a way
that mirrors geometric proofs.  The partition controls local clusters of
trapped mass, the buffer accounts for vertices lying in the separating
interface, and the separator-convolution bound is where hyperbolicity, tilted
mass transport, or a future nonamenability mechanism would enter.  Requiring
proper separators avoids the degenerate singleton partition in which each
endpoint separates itself from every other endpoint.  A plain
small-cardinality separator is not enough: the relevant quantity is the
two-point weight \(U_i^p(z)U_j^p(z)\), normalized by \(\chiBar_p|K|\).
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Local separator-convolution property]
\label{def:local-separator-convolution}
A bounded-degree graph \(G\) has the local separator-convolution property near
\(\pc\) if for every \(\delta>0\) there are \(R<\infty\) and \(p_0<\pc\) such
that, for every \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\),
there is a buffered partition
\[
  K=K_0\sqcup K_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup K_m
\]
and proper path separators \(W_{ij}\), \(i,j\ge1\), \(i\ne j\), such that
\[
  \operatorname{diam}(K_i)\le R\qquad (1\le i\le m),
\]
\[
  \mathcal B_p(K_0;K)\le\delta,
  \qquad
  \mathcal C_p(K_1,\ldots,K_m;W)\le\delta .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Local separator-convolution criterion]
\label{prop:local-separator-convolution}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, and of bounded degree.  Suppose that
\[
  \chiBar_p\to\infty\qquad \text{as }p\uparrow\pc
\]
and that \(G\) has the local separator-convolution property near \(\pc\).
Then finite-set escape holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\Delta\) be a degree bound and fix \(\delta>0\).  Let \(R\) and \(p_0\)
be supplied by Definition~\ref{def:local-separator-convolution}.  Put
\[
  V_R=1+\Delta\sum_{\ell=0}^{R-1}(\Delta-1)^\ell,
\]
with the evident interpretation when \(\Delta=1\).  Every non-buffer piece has
at most \(V_R\) vertices.  Since \(\tau_p\le1\),
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{x,y\in K_i}\tau_p(x,y)
  \le
  \sum_{i=1}^m |K_i|^2
  \le
  V_R |K|.
\]
Increasing \(p_0\) if necessary, the divergence of \(\chiBar_p\) gives
\[
  \frac{V_R}{\chiBar_p}\le\delta
  \qquad (p\in[p_0,\pc)).
\]
For such \(p\), the buffer mass and separator-convolution mass are at most
\(\delta\), and the normalized same-piece mass is at most \(\delta\).  The
proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:separator-convolution-criterion} gives
\[
  \frac{1}{|K|}\sum_{x,y\in K}Q_p(x,y)\le3\delta
\]
uniformly over finite \(K\).  Since \(\delta\) is arbitrary, finite-set escape
follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Local separator intermediate theorem]
\label{thm:local-separator-intermediate}
Let \(G\) be connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive, nonamenable, and of
bounded degree.  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
  \item \(G\) has the local separator-convolution property near \(\pc\);
  \item \(\limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}(\pc-p)\chiBar_p<\infty\).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
  \pc(G)<p_{2\to2}(G).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For quasi-transitive graphs, \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\).
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-separator-convolution} gives finite-set escape.
The mean-field assumption is \eqref{eq:mf}, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:hutchcroft-criterion} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This local version removes the same-piece tautology from the abstract
separator criterion.  Once the pieces have uniformly bounded diameter, their
internal contribution is killed by the divergence of \(\chiBar_p\).  The
remaining nontrivial work is to find a small buffer and to control the proper
separator-convolution term.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Two-replica finite-set profile]
\label{def:two-replica-profile}
For \(p<\pc\) and finite non-empty \(K\subset V\), define
\[
  \mathcal R_p(K)
  =
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p |K|}
  \sum_{z\in V}\left(\sum_{x\in K}\tau_p(x,z)\right)^2
  =
  \frac{\norm{T_p\mathbf 1_K}_2^2}{\chiBar_p |K|}.
\]
Let
\[
  \mathcal R_p^*=\sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}\mathcal R_p(K).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-set escape is sublinear two-replica escape]
\label{prop:fe-iff-sublinear-two-replica}
Let \(Q\) be a positive symmetric kernel on \(V\) satisfying
\(\sup_x\sum_yQ(x,y)\le1\).  Define
\[
  \eta(Q)=
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_K}{Q\mathbf 1_K}}{|K|}
\]
and
\[
  \rho(Q)=
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}
  \frac{\norm{Q\mathbf 1_K}_2^2}{|K|}.
\]
Then
\[
  \eta(Q)^2\le \rho(Q)\le \sqrt{6\eta(Q)} .
\]
Consequently, for the percolation kernels \(Q_p=T_p/\chiBar_p\),
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\eta(Q_p)=0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}=0 .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For every finite non-empty \(K\),
\[
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_K}{Q\mathbf 1_K}}{|K|}
  \le
  \frac{\norm{\mathbf 1_K}_2\norm{Q\mathbf 1_K}_2}{|K|}
  =
  \left(\frac{\norm{Q\mathbf 1_K}_2^2}{|K|}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Taking suprema gives \(\eta(Q)^2\le\rho(Q)\).

For the converse bound, fix \(K\) and put \(g=Q\mathbf 1_K\) and
\[
  a=\frac{\norm{g}_2^2}{|K|}.
\]
Since \(Q\) has row and column sums at most one, \(0\le g\le1\) and
\(\norm{g}_1\le |K|\), so \(0\le a\le1\).  If \(a=0\) there is nothing to
prove.  Let
\[
  H=\{y\in V:g(y)\ge a/2\}.
\]
This set is finite, because \(g\in\ell^1(V)\).  Since \(g^2\le g\) on \(H\)
and \(g^2\le (a/2)g\) on \(V\setminus H\),
\[
  a|K|
  =
  \sum_y g(y)^2
  \le
  \sum_{y\in H}g(y)+\frac a2\sum_{y\notin H}g(y)
  \le
  \sum_{y\in H}g(y)+\frac a2|K|.
\]
Thus
\[
  \sum_{y\in H}g(y)\ge \frac a2|K|.
\]
Also \(|H|\le2|K|/a\), because \(g\ge a/2\) on \(H\) and
\(\norm{g}_1\le |K|\).  Put \(U=K\cup H\).  Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \eta(Q)
  &\ge
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_U}{Q\mathbf 1_U}}{|U|}
  \ge
  \frac{\sum_{y\in H}\sum_{x\in K}Q(y,x)}{|K|+|H|}  \\
  &=
  \frac{\sum_{y\in H}g(y)}{|K|+|H|}
  \ge
  \frac{(a/2)|K|}{|K|(1+2/a)}
  \ge
  \frac{a^2}{6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since this holds for every \(K\), \(\rho(Q)\le\sqrt{6\eta(Q)}\).

For \(Q=Q_p\),
\[
  \rho(Q_p)
  =
  \sup_K\frac{\norm{Q_p\mathbf 1_K}_2^2}{|K|}
  =
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
The displayed equivalence follows from the two inequalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite-set escape is stable under squaring]
\label{cor:escape-stable-under-squaring}
Let \(Q\) be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:fe-iff-sublinear-two-replica}, and
let
\[
  Q^2(x,y)=\sum_{z\in V}Q(x,z)Q(z,y).
\]
Then \(Q^2\) is again positive, symmetric, and has row sums at most one, and
\[
  \eta(Q)^2\le \eta(Q^2)\le \sqrt{6\eta(Q)} .
\]
Consequently, for any family \(Q_\alpha\) of such kernels,
\[
  \eta(Q_\alpha)\to0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \eta(Q_\alpha^2)\to0 .
\]
For \(Q_p=T_p/\chiBar_p\),
\[
  \eta(Q_p^2)=\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The row-sum bound follows from Tonelli's theorem:
\[
  \sum_yQ^2(x,y)
  =
  \sum_z Q(x,z)\sum_yQ(z,y)
  \le
  \sum_zQ(x,z)\le1 .
\]
Symmetry and positivity are immediate.  Moreover, for every finite \(K\),
\[
  \ip{\mathbf 1_K}{Q^2\mathbf 1_K}
  =
  \ip{Q\mathbf 1_K}{Q\mathbf 1_K}
  =
  \norm{Q\mathbf 1_K}_2^2 .
\]
Thus \(\eta(Q^2)=\rho(Q)\), and the two-sided estimate is exactly
Proposition~\ref{prop:fe-iff-sublinear-two-replica}.  The equivalence for a
family follows from this estimate.  The final identity is the computation
already used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:fe-iff-sublinear-two-replica}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The second half of the proof is constructive.  If
\(\norm{Q\mathbf 1_K}_2^2/|K|=a>0\), then the level set
\[
  H=\{Q\mathbf 1_K\ge a/2\}
\]
has \(|H|\le2|K|/a\), and \(U=K\cup H\) satisfies
\[
  \frac{\ip{\mathbf 1_U}{Q\mathbf 1_U}}{|U|}\ge \frac{a^2}{6}.
\]
Thus large two-replica mass cannot hide only as an external \(L^2\) effect:
one thresholding step converts it into an ordinary finite-set trapping
witness.  Equivalently, the two-replica obstruction is precisely finite-set
trapping for the squared kernel \(Q^2\).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Square-kernel trapping is long range]
\label{prop:square-trapping-long-range}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that
\(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\).  For \(R<\infty\), let
\[
  V_R=\sup_{x\in V}|B(x,R)|<\infty .
\]
Then, for \(i=1,2\),
\[
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}
  \frac{1}{|K|}
  \sum_{\substack{x,y\in K\\ d(x,y)\le R}} Q_p^i(x,y)
  \le
  \frac{V_R}{\chiBar_p},
\]
where \(Q_p^1=Q_p\) and \(Q_p^2\) denotes the squared kernel.
Consequently, if \(\eta(Q_{p_n}^2)\ge\epsilon>0\) along
\(p_n\uparrow\pc\), then there are finite non-empty \(K_n\subset V\) such
that, for every fixed \(R<\infty\),
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}
  \frac{1}{|K_n|}
  \sum_{\substack{x,y\in K_n\\ d(x,y)>R}}Q_{p_n}^2(x,y)
  \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2} .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For \(i=1\), \(Q_p(x,y)=\tau_p(x,y)/\chiBar_p\le1/\chiBar_p\).  For the
squared kernel,
\[
  Q_p^2(x,y)
  =
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p^2}\sum_{z\in V}\tau_p(x,z)\tau_p(z,y)
  \le
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p^2}\sum_{z\in V}\tau_p(x,z)
  \le
  \frac1{\chiBar_p}.
\]
Thus, for each fixed \(x\), the contribution from \(y\in K\cap B(x,R)\) is at
most \(V_R/\chiBar_p\).  Summing over \(x\in K\) and dividing by \(|K|\)
proves the displayed local bound.

If \(\eta(Q_{p_n}^2)\ge\epsilon\), choose \(K_n\) so that
\[
  \frac1{|K_n|}\sum_{x,y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}^2(x,y)\ge\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
Subtracting the local bound with fixed \(R\), and using
\(\chiBar_{p_n}\to\infty\), gives the claimed long-range lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Long-range square trapping has a far root leg]
\label{prop:square-trapping-far-root-leg}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:square-trapping-long-range}, suppose
that \(\eta(Q_{p_n}^2)\ge\epsilon>0\) along \(p_n\uparrow\pc\).  Then there
are finite non-empty \(K_n\subset V\) such that, for every fixed
\(R<\infty\),
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}
  \frac1{|K_n|}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(\sum_{\substack{x\in K_n\\ d(x,z)>R}}Q_{p_n}(x,z)\right)
  \left(\sum_{y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}(z,y)\right)
  \ge \frac{\epsilon}{4}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(K_n\) as in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:square-trapping-long-range}, so that
\[
  \frac1{|K_n|}\sum_{x,y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}^2(x,y)\ge\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
The conclusion of Proposition~\ref{prop:square-trapping-long-range} gives,
for every fixed \(R\),
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}
  \frac1{|K_n|}
  \sum_{\substack{x,y\in K_n\\ d(x,y)>2R}}Q_{p_n}^2(x,y)
  \ge \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
Now fix \(n\) and write \(Q=Q_{p_n}\), \(K=K_n\).  Expanding the squared
kernel and using the triangle inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\sum_{\substack{x,y\in K\\ d(x,y)>2R}}Q^2(x,y) \\
  &=
  \sum_{z\in V}\sum_{x,y\in K}
  \mathbf 1\{d(x,y)>2R\}Q(x,z)Q(z,y)  \\
  &\le
  2\sum_{z\in V}
  \left(\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\ d(x,z)>R}}Q(x,z)\right)
  \left(\sum_{y\in K}Q(z,y)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, if \(d(x,y)>2R\), then at least one of \(d(x,z)>R\) and
\(d(y,z)>R\) holds.  Divide by \(|K_n|\), take \(\liminf\), and use the
previous display.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Far-root square mass remains after deleting bounded neighborhoods]
\label{cor:far-root-square-mass}
Under the assumptions of
Proposition~\ref{prop:square-trapping-far-root-leg}, the sets \(K_n\) may be
chosen so that, for every fixed \(R<\infty\),
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}
  \frac1{|K_n|}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(\sum_{\substack{x\in K_n\\ d(x,z)>R}}Q_{p_n}(x,z)\right)^2
  \ge \frac{\epsilon^2}{16}.
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
  \mathcal R_p^{>R}(K)
  =
  \frac1{\chiBar_p|K|}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\ d(x,z)>R}}\tau_p(x,z)\right)^2,
\]
then
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}
  \frac{\mathcal R_{p_n}^{>R}(K_n)}{\chiBar_{p_n}}
  \ge \frac{\epsilon^2}{16}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the sets \(K_n\) supplied by
Proposition~\ref{prop:square-trapping-far-root-leg}.  Fix \(R\), and write
\[
  u_n(z)=\sum_{y\in K_n}Q_{p_n}(z,y),
  \qquad
  u_{n,R}(z)=
  \sum_{\substack{x\in K_n\\ d(x,z)>R}}Q_{p_n}(x,z).
\]
The proposition gives
\[
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ip{u_{n,R}}{u_n}}{|K_n|}
  \ge \frac{\epsilon}{4}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
  \norm{u_n}_2^2
  =
  \ip{\mathbf 1_{K_n}}{Q_{p_n}^2\mathbf 1_{K_n}}
  \le |K_n|,
\]
because \(Q_{p_n}^2\) has row sums at most one.  Cauchy--Schwarz therefore
gives
\[
  \frac{\ip{u_{n,R}}{u_n}}{|K_n|}
  \le
  \left(\frac{\norm{u_{n,R}}_2^2}{|K_n|}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Taking \(\liminf\) proves the first display.  The equivalence with
\(\mathcal R_p^{>R}\) follows by substituting
\(Q_p=\chiBar_p^{-1}T_p\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Far-leg square criterion]
\label{prop:far-leg-square-criterion}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that
\(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\).  For \(R<\infty\), define
\[
  \Theta_p(R)=
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{>R}(K)}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
Then
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}=0
\]
if and only if for every \(\delta>0\) there are \(R<\infty\) and
\(p_0<\pc\) such that
\[
  \Theta_p(R)\le\delta\qquad(p\in[p_0,\pc)).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The forward implication is immediate from
\(\mathcal R_p^{>R}(K)\le\mathcal R_p(K)\).

For the converse, fix \(R\), \(p<\pc\), and a finite non-empty \(K\).  Write
\[
  Q_p\mathbf 1_K=u_{\le R}+u_{>R},
\]
where
\[
  u_{\le R}(z)=\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\le R}}Q_p(x,z),
  \qquad
  u_{>R}(z)=\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)>R}}Q_p(x,z).
\]
Let \(V_R=\sup_x|B(x,R)|\).  Since \(Q_p(x,z)\le\chiBar_p^{-1}\), the vector
\(u_{\le R}\) is supported on \(\{z:d(z,K)\le R\}\), which has size at most
\(V_R|K|\), and satisfies \(u_{\le R}(z)\le V_R/\chiBar_p\).  Hence
\[
  \frac{\norm{u_{\le R}}_2^2}{|K|}
  \le
  \frac{V_R^3}{\chiBar_p^2}.
\]
Also
\[
  \frac{\norm{u_{>R}}_2^2}{|K|}
  =
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{>R}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le \Theta_p(R).
\]
Therefore
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  =
  \frac{\norm{Q_p\mathbf 1_K}_2^2}{|K|}
  \le
  2\frac{V_R^3}{\chiBar_p^2}+2\Theta_p(R).
\]
If the displayed far-leg condition holds, first choose \(R,p_0\) so that
\(\Theta_p(R)\le\delta/4\) for \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\), and then increase \(p_0\)
so that \(2V_R^3/\chiBar_p^2\le\delta/2\) on the same interval.  Taking the
supremum over \(K\) gives \(\mathcal R_p^*/\chiBar_p\le\delta\) near
\(\pc\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Tail-limit form of far-leg tightness]
\label{cor:far-leg-tail-limit}
Under the hypotheses and notation of
Proposition~\ref{prop:far-leg-square-criterion},
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}=0
\]
if and only if
\[
  \lim_{R\to\infty}\limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\Theta_p(R)=0 .
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For each fixed \(p\), the function \(R\mapsto \Theta_p(R)\) is non-increasing,
because the summands defining \(\mathcal R_p^{>R}(K)\) are nonnegative and the
set \(\{x\in K:d(x,z)>R\}\) decreases with \(R\).  Thus
\[
  L(R)=\limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\Theta_p(R)
\]
is non-increasing in \(R\).

If \(\mathcal R_p^*/\chiBar_p\to0\), the far-leg condition in
Proposition~\ref{prop:far-leg-square-criterion} implies that for every
\(\delta>0\) there is \(R<\infty\) with \(L(R)\le\delta\).  Hence
\(\lim_{R\to\infty}L(R)=0\).

Conversely, if \(\lim_{R\to\infty}L(R)=0\), then for every \(\delta>0\) there
is \(R<\infty\) with \(L(R)<\delta\).  By the definition of the limsup in
\(p\), there is \(p_0<\pc\) such that \(\Theta_p(R)\le\delta\) for all
\(p\in[p_0,\pc)\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:far-leg-square-criterion} gives the
claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Annular square profiles]
\label{def:annular-square-profile}
For \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), define
\[
  \mathcal R_p^I(K)
  =
  \frac1{\chiBar_p|K|}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(
    \sum_{\substack{x\in K\\ d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z)
  \right)^2
\]
and
\[
  \Theta_p(I)=
  \sup_{K\subset V\text{ finite non-empty}}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^I(K)}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
Thus \(\Theta_p((R,\infty))=\Theta_p(R)\).
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Annular profile size bounds]
\label{lem:annular-profile-size-bounds}
For every \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), every \(p<\pc\), and every finite
non-empty \(K\subset V\),
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^I(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \min\left\{1,\frac{|K|}{\chiBar_p}\right\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put
\[
  s_z=\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z).
\]
Since \(\sum_x\tau_p(x,z)\le\chiBar_p\) and
\(\sum_zs_z\le\chiBar_p|K|\),
\[
  \sum_zs_z^2\le \chiBar_p\sum_zs_z\le \chiBar_p^2|K|.
\]
This gives \(\mathcal R_p^I(K)/\chiBar_p\le1\).
Also, by Cauchy--Schwarz and \(\tau_p(x,z)^2\le\tau_p(x,z)\),
\[
  s_z^2
  \le
  |K|\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z)^2
  \le
  |K|\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z).
\]
After summing over \(z\), this gives
\[
  \sum_zs_z^2\le \chiBar_p|K|^2,
\]
and hence \(\mathcal R_p^I(K)/\chiBar_p\le |K|/\chiBar_p\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Weighted annular profiles reduce to level sets]
\label{lem:weighted-annular-profile-level-sets}
Let \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), let \(p<\pc\), and let
\(w:V\to[0,\infty)\) be finitely supported and non-zero.  Then
\[
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p^2\norm{w}_1\norm{w}_\infty}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(
    \sum_{\substack{x\in V\\d(x,z)\in I}}w(x)\tau_p(x,z)
  \right)^2
  \le
  \Theta_p(I).
\]
In particular, if \(0\le w\le1\), then the factor
\(\norm{w}_\infty\) may be omitted.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(M=\norm{w}_\infty\), and for \(0\le t<M\) let
\[
  K_t=\{x\in V:w(x)>t\}
\]
and
\[
  g_t(z)=
  \sum_{\substack{x\in K_t\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z).
\]
Then \(w(x)=\int_0^M\mathbf 1_{\{x\in K_t\}}\,dt\), and hence
\[
  s_z:=
  \sum_{\substack{x\in V\\d(x,z)\in I}}w(x)\tau_p(x,z)
  =
  \int_0^M g_t(z)\,dt .
\]
Since
\[
  \int_0^M |K_t|\,dt=\norm{w}_1,
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz gives, for every \(z\),
\[
  s_z^2
  \le
  \norm{w}_1
  \int_{\{0\le t<M:K_t\ne\varnothing\}}\frac{g_t(z)^2}{|K_t|}\,dt .
\]
After summing over \(z\), Definition~\ref{def:annular-square-profile} gives
\[
  \sum_zs_z^2
  \le
  \norm{w}_1
  \int_0^M
  \chiBar_p^2\Theta_p(I)\,dt
  =
  \chiBar_p^2\norm{w}_1\norm{w}_\infty\Theta_p(I).
\]
Dividing by
\(\chiBar_p^2\norm{w}_1\norm{w}_\infty\) proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Weighted annular mass lower bound]
\label{lem:weighted-annular-mass-lower-bound}
Let \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), let \(p<\pc\), let \(A,Y\subset V\) be finite
non-empty sets, and let \(w:A\to[0,1]\) satisfy
\[
  S:=\sum_{a\in A}w(a)>0.
\]
If \(m>0\) and
\[
  \sum_{\substack{y\in Y\\d(y,a)\in I}}\tau_p(y,a)\ge m
  \qquad(a\in A\text{ with }w(a)>0),
\]
then
\[
  \Theta_p(I)\ge \frac{m^2S}{\chiBar_p^2|Y|}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Extend \(w\) by zero off \(A\), and put
\[
  s_y=\sum_{\substack{a\in A\\d(y,a)\in I}}w(a)\tau_p(y,a)
  \qquad(y\in Y).
\]
The mass assumption gives
\[
  \sum_{y\in Y}s_y\ge mS.
\]
Thus Cauchy--Schwarz yields
\[
  \sum_{y\in Y}s_y^2\ge\frac{m^2S^2}{|Y|}.
\]
Since \(0\le w\le1\), Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-annular-profile-level-sets}
implies
\[
  \Theta_p(I)
  \ge
  \frac{1}{\chiBar_p^2S}
  \sum_{z\in V}
  \left(
    \sum_{\substack{a\in A\\d(a,z)\in I}}w(a)\tau_p(a,z)
  \right)^2
  \ge
  \frac{m^2S}{\chiBar_p^2|Y|}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Annular root layers]
\label{def:annular-root-layers}
For \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), \(0\le\lambda\le1\), and a finite
non-empty \(K\subset V\), define
\[
  Z_p^I(K,\lambda)
  =
  \left\{
    z\in V:
    \sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z)
    \ge \lambda\chiBar_p
  \right\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Annular square mass creates root layers]
\label{lem:annular-root-layer-extraction}
For every \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), every \(0\le\lambda\le1\), every
\(p<\pc\), and every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\),
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^I(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \lambda+\frac{|Z_p^I(K,\lambda)|}{|K|}.
\]
Consequently, if \(\mathcal R_p^I(K)/\chiBar_p\ge\sigma>\lambda\), then
\[
  |Z_p^I(K,\lambda)|\ge(\sigma-\lambda)|K|.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put
\[
  s_z=\sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z),
  \qquad
  Z=Z_p^I(K,\lambda).
\]
As above, \(s_z\le\chiBar_p\) for every \(z\), and
\(\sum_zs_z\le\chiBar_p|K|\).  On \(V\setminus Z\),
\(s_z^2\le\lambda\chiBar_p s_z\), while on \(Z\),
\(s_z^2\le\chiBar_p^2\).  Hence
\[
  \sum_zs_z^2
  \le
  \lambda\chiBar_p^2|K|+\chiBar_p^2|Z|.
\]
Dividing by \(\chiBar_p^2|K|\) gives the first claim, and the second follows
immediately.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted annular far-leg criterion]
\label{prop:weighted-annular-far-leg}
Fix \(R<\infty\), and let \(\{I_j:j\in J\}\) be a countable partition of
\((R,\infty)\).  If \(a_j>0\) and
\[
  A=\sum_{j\in J}a_j^{-1}<\infty,
\]
then for every \(p<\pc\),
\[
  \Theta_p(R)
  \le
  A\sum_{j\in J}a_j\Theta_p(I_j),
\]
with the convention that the right-hand side may be infinite.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix a finite non-empty \(K\).  Write
\[
  u_j(z)=
  \sum_{\substack{x\in K\\ d(x,z)\in I_j}}Q_p(x,z).
\]
Then
\[
  \sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)>R}}Q_p(x,z)=\sum_{j\in J}u_j(z)
\]
pointwise.  Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
  \left(\sum_{j\in J}u_j(z)\right)^2
  \le
  \left(\sum_{j\in J}a_j^{-1}\right)
  \left(\sum_{j\in J}a_j u_j(z)^2\right)
  =
  A\sum_{j\in J}a_j u_j(z)^2 .
\]
For countable \(J\), apply this first to finite partial sums and then use
monotone convergence.
Summing over \(z\), dividing by \(|K|\), and taking the supremum over \(K\)
gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dyadic annular sufficient condition]
\label{cor:dyadic-annular-far-leg}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  For \(j\ge J\), let \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\).  Suppose that
for some \(\alpha>0\),
\[
  \lim_{J\to\infty}
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}\Theta_p(I_j)=0.
\]
Then
\[
  \lim_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}=0 .
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:weighted-annular-far-leg} with
\(R=2^J\), \(a_j=2^{\alpha(j-J)}\), and
\[
  A=\sum_{j\ge J}2^{-\alpha(j-J)}=\frac{1}{1-2^{-\alpha}}.
\]
The displayed assumption implies
\(\lim_{J\to\infty}\limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\Theta_p(2^J)=0\).  The
tail-limit criterion, Corollary~\ref{cor:far-leg-tail-limit}, gives the
claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Dyadic annular obstruction]
\label{prop:dyadic-annular-obstruction}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  If
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}>0,
\]
then there is \(\epsilon>0\) such that for every \(\alpha>0\),
\[
  \liminf_{J\to\infty}
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
    \Theta_p((2^j,2^{j+1}])
  \ge (1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon .
\]
More concretely, for every \(\alpha>0\), every integer \(J\ge0\), and every
\(p_0<\pc\), there are \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty
\(K\subset V\) such that, writing \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\),
\[
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \ge (1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon .
\]
The same \(p\) and \(K\) may be chosen so that
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{>2^J}(K)}{\chiBar_p}>2\epsilon,
  \qquad
  |K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let
\[
  L=\lim_{R\to\infty}\limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\Theta_p(R).
\]
If \(L=0\), Corollary~\ref{cor:far-leg-tail-limit} gives
\(\mathcal R_p^*/\chiBar_p\to0\), contradicting the hypothesis.  Hence
\(L>0\).  Choose \(\epsilon>0\) with \(2\epsilon<L\).

Fix \(\alpha>0\), an integer \(J\ge0\), and \(p_0<\pc\).  Since
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\Theta_p(2^J)\ge L>2\epsilon,
\]
there is \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) such that \(\Theta_p(2^J)>2\epsilon\).  By the
definition of the supremum, there is a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) with
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{>2^J}(K)}{\chiBar_p}>2\epsilon .
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-profile-size-bounds}, applied to
\(I=(2^J,\infty)\), gives \(|K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p\).
For \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\), the annuli \(I_j\), \(j\ge J\), partition
\((2^J,\infty)\).  Applying the weighted Cauchy--Schwarz estimate from the
proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:weighted-annular-far-leg} to this same \(K\),
with \(a_j=2^{\alpha(j-J)}\), gives
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{>2^J}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \frac{1}{1-2^{-\alpha}}
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}.
\]
The concrete lower bound follows.  Since
\(\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)/\chiBar_p\le\Theta_p(I_j)\), the same construction
also gives the stated \(\liminf_J\limsup_p\) obstruction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted annular root-layer obstruction]
\label{prop:weighted-root-layer-obstruction}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  If
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}>0,
\]
then there is \(\epsilon>0\) such that the following holds.  For every
\(0<\alpha<\beta\), every integer \(J\ge0\), and every \(p_0<\pc\), there
are \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) with
\[
  |K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p
\]
such that, writing \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\) and
\[
  \lambda_j
  =
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}(1-2^{-\alpha})(1-2^{\alpha-\beta})
  2^{-\beta(j-J)},
\]
we have
\[
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{|Z_p^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j)|}{|K|}
  \ge
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}(1-2^{-\alpha}) .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\epsilon\) be given by
Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadic-annular-obstruction}.  Fix
\(0<\alpha<\beta\), \(J\ge0\), and \(p_0<\pc\), and apply the concrete part of
that proposition with this \(\alpha\).  We get \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite
non-empty \(K\subset V\) such that \(|K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p\) and
\[
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \ge
  (1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon .
\]
Set
\[
  c=(1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon,
  \qquad
  \lambda_j=\frac{c}{2}(1-2^{\alpha-\beta})2^{-\beta(j-J)} .
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-root-layer-extraction} gives, for every \(j\ge J\),
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \lambda_j+\frac{|Z_p^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j)|}{|K|}.
\]
Multiplying by \(2^{\alpha(j-J)}\) and summing over \(j\ge J\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
  c
  &\le
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}\lambda_j
  +
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{|Z_p^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j)|}{|K|}   \\
  &=
  \frac{c}{2}
  +
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{|Z_p^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j)|}{|K|}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Annular incidence layers]
\label{def:annular-incidence-layers}
For \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), \(m\ge0\), and finite non-empty
\(K\subset V\), define
\[
  \mathcal N^I(K,m)
  =
  \left\{
    z\in V:
    |\{x\in K:d(x,z)\in I\}|\ge m
  \right\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Root layers have large deterministic incidence]
\label{lem:root-layer-incidence}
For every \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), every \(0\le\lambda\le1\), every
\(p<\pc\), and every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\),
\[
  Z_p^I(K,\lambda)
  \subseteq
  \mathcal N^I(K,\lambda\chiBar_p).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(z\in Z_p^I(K,\lambda)\), then
\[
  \lambda\chiBar_p
  \le
  \sum_{\substack{x\in K\\d(x,z)\in I}}\tau_p(x,z)
  \le
  |\{x\in K:d(x,z)\in I\}|,
\]
since \(\tau_p(x,z)\le1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted annular incidence obstruction]
\label{prop:weighted-incidence-obstruction}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  If
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}>0,
\]
then there is \(\epsilon>0\) such that the following holds.  For every
\(0<\alpha<\beta\), every integer \(J\ge0\), and every \(p_0<\pc\), there
are \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) with
\[
  |K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p
\]
such that, writing \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\) and
\[
  m_j
  =
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}(1-2^{-\alpha})(1-2^{\alpha-\beta})
  2^{-\beta(j-J)}\chiBar_p,
\]
we have
\[
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{|\mathcal N^{I_j}(K,m_j)|}{|K|}
  \ge
  \frac{\epsilon}{2}(1-2^{-\alpha}) .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:weighted-root-layer-obstruction}.  Its thresholds
\(\lambda_j\) satisfy \(m_j=\lambda_j\chiBar_p\), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:root-layer-incidence} gives
\[
  Z_p^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j)\subseteq\mathcal N^{I_j}(K,m_j)
  \qquad(j\ge J).
\]
The stated lower bound follows from the lower bound in
Proposition~\ref{prop:weighted-root-layer-obstruction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-window high-incidence alternative]
\label{prop:finite-window-incidence-alternative}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  If
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}>0,
\]
then there is \(0<\epsilon\le1\) such that the following holds.  Fix
\(\alpha>0\), an integer \(H\ge0\), an integer \(J\ge0\), and
\(p_0<\pc\).  Put \(I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}]\) and
\[
  c=(1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon .
\]
There are \(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\), with
\[
  |K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p,
\]
such that at least one of the following alternatives holds:
\[
  \sum_{j>J+H}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \ge \frac{c}{2},
  \tag{T}
  \label{eq:finite-window-tail-alt}
\]
or, writing
\[
  \lambda_j=\frac{c}{4(H+1)}2^{-\alpha(j-J)}
  \qquad(J\le j\le J+H),
\]
we have
\[
  \sum_{j=J}^{J+H}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{|\mathcal N^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j\chiBar_p)|}{|K|}
  \ge \frac{c}{4}.
  \tag{W}
  \label{eq:finite-window-incidence-alt}
\]
Moreover, for every \(M<\infty\) there exists \(p_1<\pc\), depending on
\(\alpha,H,M,\epsilon\), such that if \(p_0\ge p_1\) and
\eqref{eq:finite-window-incidence-alt} holds, then
\(\lambda_j\chiBar_p\ge M\) for every \(J\le j\le J+H\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\epsilon\) be the constant from
Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadic-annular-obstruction}, shrunk if necessary so
that \(\epsilon\le1\).  Applying the concrete part of that proposition gives
\(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\), with
\(|K|>2\epsilon\chiBar_p\), such that
\[
  \sum_{j\ge J}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \ge c.
\]
If \eqref{eq:finite-window-tail-alt} holds, there is nothing to prove.  If it
does not hold, then
\[
  \sum_{j=J}^{J+H}2^{\alpha(j-J)}
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \ge \frac{c}{2}.
\]
For \(J\le j\le J+H\), Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-root-layer-extraction} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:root-layer-incidence} give
\[
  \frac{\mathcal R_p^{I_j}(K)}{\chiBar_p}
  \le
  \lambda_j+
  \frac{|\mathcal N^{I_j}(K,\lambda_j\chiBar_p)|}{|K|}.
\]
Since
\[
  \sum_{j=J}^{J+H}2^{\alpha(j-J)}\lambda_j=\frac{c}{4},
\]
the finite-window incidence bound follows.

Finally, for \(J\le j\le J+H\),
\[
  \lambda_j\ge \frac{c}{4(H+1)}2^{-\alpha H}.
\]
Since \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as \(p\uparrow\pc\), choose \(p_1<\pc\) so that
\[
  \frac{c}{4(H+1)}2^{-\alpha H}\chiBar_p\ge M
  \qquad(p\in[p_1,\pc)).
\]
This proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Incidence layer volume bound]
\label{lem:incidence-layer-volume-bound}
Let \(G\) be locally finite.  For \(I\subseteq[0,\infty)\), put
\[
  V(I)=\sup_{x\in V}|\{z\in V:d(x,z)\in I\}|.
\]
Then for every finite non-empty \(K\subset V\) and every \(m>0\),
\[
  \frac{|\mathcal N^I(K,m)|}{|K|}
  \le
  \frac{V(I)}{m},
\]
with the convention that the bound is trivial if \(V(I)=\infty\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each \(z\in\mathcal N^I(K,m)\) contributes at least \(m\) incidences
\((x,z)\) with \(x\in K\) and \(d(x,z)\in I\).  Therefore
\[
  m|\mathcal N^I(K,m)|
  \le
  |\{(x,z)\in K\times V:d(x,z)\in I\}|
  \le
  |K|V(I).
\]
Divide by \(m|K|\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Fixed windows cannot carry the obstruction near criticality]
\label{prop:fixed-window-obstruction-escapes}
Let \(G\) have bounded degree, and suppose that \(\chiBar_p\to\infty\) as
\(p\uparrow\pc\).  If
\[
  \limsup_{p\uparrow\pc}\frac{\mathcal R_p^*}{\chiBar_p}>0,
\]
then there is \(0<\epsilon\le1\) such that the following holds.  Fix
\(\alpha>0\), integers \(J,H\ge0\), and put
\[
  c=(1-2^{-\alpha})\epsilon,
  \qquad
  I_j=(2^j,2^{j+1}].
\]
There is \(p_1<\pc\) such that for every \(p_0\in[p_1,\pc)\) there are
\(p\in[p_0,\pc)\) and a finite non-empty \(K\subset V\), with
\[
